We address two key research questions for this challenge by presenting new approaches to representing utterances semantically and clustering them effectively. Firstly, we develop a multi-task pre-training strategy that leverages a large amount of unlabeled data in conjunction with labeled external data for representation learning. Secondly, we design a new contrastive loss to capitalize on self-supervising signals from unlabeled data for clustering. Experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate the superior performance of our method over existing approaches in both unsupervised and semi-supervised settings.

The classical universal bundle functor W mapping from the category of simplicial groups in C to the category of simplicial sets in C lifts to a monadic structure on the category of simplicial groups in C, and this extension holds for simplicial algebras defined by any Lawvere theory that includes group theory.
In our analysis, we demonstrate that a finite group of order $r$ possesses no more than $$7.3722\cdot r^{\frac{\log_2r}{4}+1.5315}$$ subgroups.

This study re-examines the Adler-Bobenko-Suris H2 equation. The equation has a direct linear relationship with the Cauchy matrix scheme variables S0,0 and S1,0. A detailed analysis is provided on the coupled system of these variables in terms of 3D consistency, Lax pair, bilinear form and continuum limits. The analysis reveals that the variable S1,0 itself adheres to a 9-point lattice equation and upon continuum limiting, it is related to the Lax pair's eigenfunction of the Korteweg-de Vries equation.

This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that low-frequency relationships are easily distorted, leading to model propagation of errors. To address this, we developed Frequency-Aware Hard example Mining (F AHM), a method that selects difficult instances in both high and low-frequency categories. This technique has proven successful in reducing false positives and improving performance overall. Furthermore, we found that our method can be adapted in such a way that only hard examples from low-frequency relationships are mined, making it computationally efficient. Experiment results show that our method significantly reduces false positives and maintains a strong AP performance on the VRD dataset.

A new measure, referred to as quantum correlation cost (QCC), quantifies the amount of quantum correlation employed in weak measurement procedures utilizing the trace norm. It has been demonstrated that the QCC is a valid quantum operation whose trace norm serves as a measure of the operator's distance from orthogonality and that it possesses the ability to detect quantum correlation even within stationary states. Furthermore, research has shown that the QCC can distinguish any two distinct quantum states, an ability that surpasses that of the von Neumann entropy-based measure, particularly in cases involving states with low entropy but high correlation values. Lastly, the QCC has been found to be capable of detecting entanglement within multipartite systems.

Artificial intelligence's interest in socially-aware agents is increasing. To address this, systems capable of deciphering diverse social interactions are needed. Understanding social relationships in a visual setting requires not only object recognition but also an in-depth comprehension of relationships and attributes within that scene. An explicit knowledge graph can be employed to model human connections and attributes, allowing for advanced reasoning. A novel neural network is introduced that can generate a structured graph of social relationships from an input image. This network, called the Social Relationship Graph Generation Network (SRG-GN), utilizes GRUs to iteratively refine social connection representations by combining visual scene and attribute context. By enabling message exchange between nodes in the graph, the network outperforms existing social relationship recognition methods.

Capturing long-range relationships in scene understanding tasks is a crucial goal in computer vision. While CNNs excel in many vision tasks, they have limitations in modelling global, structured relationships due to their localized nature. A fully connected graph like the self-attention mechanism in CNNs (e.g. 2D) is beneficial, however it comes with a steep computational cost and impractical memory demands. The key issue here is modelling concurrent cross-attention connections in small groups, a difficulty that has held back the development of graph-based models for direct integration with CNNs. Our proposed Dynamic Graph Message Passing layer overcomes this challenge by simultaneously computing local and group-level messages, achieving a significant speedup (up to 3x) with reduced memory requirements, all while outperforming existing graph attention networks by a notable margin (5-6%) in terms of accuracy. Our innovative approach leads to the development of the CGNN network that achieves superior performance across multiple benchmark datasets, thereby demonstrating the practical value of graph-based models in computer vision.

Optimized hardware is often required in embedded systems, leading to a common operation called Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM) over integers. One efficient way to achieve this optimization is by replacing expensive generic multiplication with bit-shifts and additions in a multiplierless circuit. Our work advances the state-of-the-art in optimal MCM approaches based on Integer Linear Programming (ILP) and introduces a novel hardware cost model. This model counts one-bit adders, demonstrating a strong correlation with the number of LUTs required. Our enhanced model accommodates intermediate precision truncations, enabling significant resource savings when full precision is not essential. Additionally, we incorporate error propagation rules to ensure a specified MCM accuracy within a bounded range. Our proposed ILP models for various MCM configurations are available in full at github.com/alekseypovylai/MCM_optimization.

The intersection of quantum computing and deep neural networks has recently given rise to a growing research field, known as quantum deep learning. Despite previously being separate entities, advancements have revealed that quantum circuits share parallels with artificial neural networks, paving the way for widespread adoption. This paper delves into the foundational aspects and core principles of quantum deep learning, highlighting key breakthroughs along the way. It also explores the challenges inherent in quantum deep learning research from multiple viewpoints, followed by a discussion of prospective future directions and practical applications.

The radio frequency (RF) accelerator technology continues to be fundamental in high-energy physics (HEP) experiments, where significant progress has been made over the past decade in advancing the field. This progress could soon lead to upgraded existing facilities, enhancements to facilities still under construction (such as PIP-II), well-established proposals, or newly emerging ideas like the FCC-ee and future proton intensity upgrade at Fermilab, among others. The development of RF technology has far-reaching applications beyond HEP, as it is extensively used in science, medicine, and industry. Therefore, an extensive report by the AF7-rf topical group to Snowmass 2021 on RF accelerator technology has been prepared to cover the following key areas: an introduction to RF technology; a detailed explanation of linear accelerators including design, components, and operations; an in-depth analysis of technology and R&D programs; and case studies of specific accelerator systems, followed by a conclusion and future perspectives.

In the near future, physicists anticipate that the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) will discover new physics. However, the specific characteristics and energy thresholds of this new physics remain unknown. It's probable that insights gleaned from LHC data will require supplementary information obtained from a lepton collider to conduct a thorough investigation. This text discusses the underlying principles, accelerator layout, and detector development for a high-energy Muon Collider as well as the difficulties inherent in the machine and its detector environment.

We have determined the dispersion relations for relativistic fluid modes in various configurations - scalar, vector, and tensor - and found the differences between their behavior in divergence-based and relaxation-time-approximation models. Our comparison also shows correspondence with first-order causal theories and highlights how a specific divergence-based model can predict damped tensor waves. This aligns with kinetic theory's results. It's interesting that both hydrodynamic and holographic fluids display similar properties. These findings reinforce the feasibility of using hydrodynamics to analyze the interaction between gravitational waves and fluids.

Our research assesses whether the cosmic background of Hawking radiation from primordial black holes could be the source behind the observed excess radiowave signals. By assuming that dark matter exists entirely as these black holes, we calculated that the temperature resulting from Hawking radiation is negligible in comparison to the cosmic microwave background, primarily due to the black holes' low mass. This is caused by the emission's power law suppression of lower-energy frequencies. Although higher-mass black holes have lower-energy peaks, the intensity of Hawking radiation is still not sufficient to explain the observed signals. In an alternative scenario, we find that massive black holes may be able to emit radio waves as gas is drawn towards them, which could potentially account for the observed excess in ARCADE2 and LWA1 experiments.

Introducing the Virtual Secure Platform (VSP), a pioneering solution that brings together multi-opcode general-purpose sequential processing with Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) to enable Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMPC) at a functional level. To showcase the capabilities of VSP, we have developed a custom Instruction-Set-Architecture (ISA) and built a new instruction set, which we have implemented into a software framework. To further enhance performance, we have created an optimized hardware accelerator and demonstrated the effectiveness of VSP through a series of practical use cases, such as protecting IoT devices and facilitating secure outsourcing for computing tasks. To evaluate the processing speed, we have assembled a complete processing pipeline across three stages, and our results reveal a notable trade-off between security, output size, and processing speed, which presents a notable challenge to be addressed in future research initiatives focused on accelerating FHE-based computations.

Researchers investigate polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS) for solving specific constraint satisfaction problems, such as Maximum Independent Set or Minimum Vertex Cover on graph classes that have limited connectivity.

A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further, Romero, Wrochna, and Zivny developed a simpler PTAS for certain graph classes using the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation for maximum CSPs with constraints having specific structure.

This research is extended to more general constraint types by first reducing the computational complexity of obtaining LP relaxation lower bounds, and then developing a new scheme for CSPs with constraints that have specific structure.

The findings apply to CSPs with constraints such as clique, hole, and chordless cycle, and the results can be applied to other graph classes with approximate solutions.

Pre-trained language models possess the ability to capture syntactical information, as established in previous studies [Tenney et al., 2019, Jawahar et al., 2019, Hewitt and Manning, 2019]. Yet, the structured output of dependencies is difficult for models to replicate compared to other sequential tasks such as machine translation or part-of-speech tagging. We propose two unsupervised constituent parsing models, U2C and RNN-CRNN, that demonstrate superior performance over individual constituent parsing models, achieving a 4.1 F-measure increase over baseline models in PTB dataset. Notably, U2C's performance in F-measure (57.5) surpasses that of human annotators (54.3) in the PTB dataset. We also examine the potential of self-supervised pre-training of parsing models, as well as the efficacy of fine-tuning pre-trained models on relatively under-resourced datasets such as the PAWS dataset. In another line of research, we have developed a novel unsupervised, convolutional parsing model named Chain. This innovative model analyzes sentences as a linked sequence of paragraphs, leveraging the capabilities of pre-trained models, as well as the 'paragraph' structure of sentences, to enhance parsing accuracy. Chain has surpassed the performance of traditional parsing models in the PAWS dataset, achieving a 11.6 F-measure increase. Furthermore, it exhibits considerable success in few-shot parsing on a range of languages, demonstrating

High-definition hyperspectral images possess the unique capability to distinguish between diverse objects within intricate environments by analyzing each pixel across various frequency ranges. Although HSI cameras are becoming increasingly accessible, associated algorithms have not been extensively utilized. This research delves into a novel application, specifically employing hyperspectral images for cityscape object segmentation using an unsupervised learning approach that circumvents the need for manual object classification. This method capitalizes on the rich spectral data inherent in HSI images, which facilitates efficient object segmentation within complex urban environments. By analyzing the inherent properties of HSI images and developing a corresponding segmentation framework, we demonstrate how these images can improve low-quality labels, ultimately leading to higher accuracy in object segmentation. Our results demonstrate that this technique produces competitive results and outperforms manually refined labels in certain scenarios. Moreover, the refined labels derived from HSI images contribute significantly to the enhancement of object segmentation. This research validates the significant potential of HSI images in advanced visual applications, showcasing the benefits of integrating spectral data and semantic analysis for enhanced visual task performance.

This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, the core and surface rotation speeds of this object are surprisingly similar. There are two theoretical explanations for this anomaly, depending on whether we consider the star's rapid rotation is a result of it being overfilled with planets or experiencing angular momentum redistribution. Planetary engulfment would typically occur in more massive stars, while the latter scenario could apply to less massive stars. Further research is needed to clarify the underlying cause of this star's rotation profile.

In algorithmic literature, the underlying computation model is typically implicit and assumed to be based on the RAM model. Despite being widely adopted, the RAM model lacks a solid theoretical foundation, characterized by inconsistent definitions and results. This research aims to rectify this issue by developing a new RAM model with desirable algorithmic properties and establishing a comprehensive complexity classification. Specifically, we investigated the class of problems solvable in linear time on linear-size input, which led to the discovery of an unexpected relationship between this class and the class of problems solvable through addition-based algorithms. Additionally, we obtained a comprehensive list of basic operations tractable in linear time, along with a characterization of non-tractable operations, and demonstrated that any operation with linear-time accessibility can be implemented using basic arithmetic operations with linear-time complexity.

To tackle the data sparsity problem affecting session-based recommendation models that predict the next item users will choose, researchers combined self-supervised learning with co-training. They proposed an enhanced framework by leveraging a session-based graph to create informative, not artificially sparse, data for these models. This new approach exploits internal and external session connections to produce contrastive learning, thereby preserving genuine data for superior session-based recommendation performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate the success of this innovative method in achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmark datasets.

This research presents a novel method for generating LCD codes using group rings and a standard transformation that maps group ring components to a subring of $n \times n$ matrices, resulting in LCD codes that are also group codes due to being ideals in a group ring. Under specific conditions for the group ring element $v$, the proposed construction allows for the creation of non-trivial group LCD codes, with additional constraints enabling the development of reversible group LCD codes. A variety of binary group LCD codes are presented, including optimal and reversible group LCD codes with various parameters.

We examine differential forms on an algebraic compactification of the metric graph moduli space, derived by mapping invariant differential forms from the tropical Torelli map. It's known that these invariant forms give rise to the stable real cohomology of the general linear group, a finding by Borel. We compute period integrals by integrating such forms across graph metrics and find them to be always finite and expressible as generalised Feynman integrals. Our integrals have further application in identifying non-zero homology classes in the graph complex, providing novel perspectives on the cohomology structure and forging links between graph theory, motivic Galois groups and quantum field theory.

In various object categorization tasks, particularly in visually complex conditions, it has been demonstrated that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can outperform feedforward models.  This research aimed to uncover the specific role of RNN recurrence in aiding object categorization.  We trained RNNs on an object categorization task and discovered through linear diagnostic analysis that auxiliary variables such as object position, orientation, and size are communicated through recurrence and contribute significantly to performance improvement.  This evidence confirms our hypothesis that auxiliary variables are utilized to optimize object categorization in cluttered environments.

Despite numerous studies on non-Hermitian topology, the influence of correlations remains a significant unresolved issue. We conducted an in-depth analysis of correlated non-Hermitian systems, with a particular focus on the topological characteristics of one-dimensional systems. Our results reveal that correlations cause a significant reduction in the topological classification from $\mathbb{Z}\times \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ for one-dimensional systems with a single synthetic dimension, along with $\mathrm{U(1)}$ symmetry and spin-parity symmetry. We also investigated the properties of an extended chain, which demonstrates that correlations complicate the point-gap topology and lead to an extensive phase diagram. Notably, we found several novel phases that do not exist under the independent particle scenario or in Hermitian systems. Our research employed the density matrix formulation to study dynamic correlations and spectral properties in the correlated system. We also constructed a minimal model to explicitly demonstrate the influence of correlations on the point-gap topology.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional patch antenna designs. Researchers have developed several innovative methods for creating Golay complementary arrays, leading to numerous applicable designs. This paper presents original methods for generating polyphase Golay complementary arrays, which consist of a pair of Golay complementary sequences aligned in a matrix format. We introduce two novel methods for constructing PGA's using skew cyclic matrices, allowing for the easy creation of PGA's with various sizes. Our techniques enable the direct formation of PGA's through the use of skew cyclic matrices, bypassing the need for partial spread spectrum techniques. We present four PGA's as exemplary models, which can be translated into omnidirectional radiation patterns for antennas.

Research on Higgs boson production is conducted, combining CMS data from 13 TeV LHC and previously collected data from 7 and 8 TeV LHC, totaling 104.6 fb^-1. The findings from four-lepton final state analysis provide joint constraints on Higgs boson width and its interaction with electroweak vector bosons. By applying matrix element techniques, production and decay mechanisms of Higgs boson are identified, and its sensitivity is enhanced. The constraints on non-standard interactions with electroweak vector bosons align with the standard model predictions in on-shell and off-shell regions. Assuming the standard model coupling structure, the Higgs boson width is constrained between 0.4 and 5.4 MeV, while the simulated expected range is between -8 and 12 MeV. The constraints on the Higgs boson width remain comparable with the consideration of tested non-standard interactions.

Incorporating dimensionality reduction techniques, researchers address the complexities of analyzing numerous spectral bands within bi-temporal hyperspectral images. This study proposes a cutting-edge approach using a novel deep convolutional autoencoder that fuses features across hierarchical levels and receptive fields. By utilizing an unsupervised change detection technique, it overcomes the limitations of other label-dependent methods. By integrating various techniques to extract changes from the images, it significantly outperformed current state-of-the-art methods in unsupervised change detection across diverse datasets.

Consider the set $\mathcal{S}$ of squares and let $\mathcal{W}$ be a subset of natural numbers such that when you combine an element from $\mathcal{S}$ with an element from $\mathcal{W}$, the result is always a natural number greater than or equal to $2$. The goal is to find all possible pairs $(s, w)$ such that $s + w$ is in $\mathcal{W}$ and also identify the structure of sets that have additive complements consisting of squares.

Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing a scanning tunneling microscope to investigate coupled atoms.
The examination reveals the significance of envelope anisotropy, valley interference and the location of the dopants on Heisenberg's spin exchange interaction in silicon.
The findings indicate that exchange interaction becomes immune to valley interference by arranging in-plane dopants in particular directions aligned with the crystallographic orientation, ultimately retrieving vacuum-like characteristics where the exchange interaction maximizes the overlap between donor orbitals, and the variation in pairs is minimized to less than 10-fold.
This robust exchange interaction remains over a considerable distance range, from a high-fidelity quantum computation regime influenced by Coulomb interaction to coupled donor arrays used in quantum simulations in silicon.

Several disciplines have been influenced by optimization techniques in various real-world scenarios, hence their importance is being increasingly acknowledged by the community. As a result of this growing interest, researchers have been able to develop multiple open-source frameworks for optimization, ultimately contributing to innovation in both techniques and their practical applications. In the context of this study, we introduce a novel framework, known as LibOPT, for efficiently implementing and prototyping nature-inspired optimization algorithms. By integrating 15 established techniques and 112 benchmark functions, as well as supporting 11 novel hypercomplex-based approaches, our framework surpasses others in its domain, thus marking it as a groundbreaking innovation in optimization software development. Utilizing LibOPT under the C paradigm proves to be remarkably user-friendly and adaptable, as evidenced by the inclusion of clear source-code examples demonstrating the practical usage of benchmark functions.

Given an algebraic variety X that has a transitive action from the group Aut(X), the highest degree of transitivity of this action is called the transitivity degree. This degree is denoted by the maximum value of m for which Aut(X) acts transitively m times on X. In cases where Aut(X) is m-transitive for any positive value of m, we define the transitivity degree to be infinite. This study involves determining the transitivity degree for specific varieties, such as quasi-affine toric varieties, and homogeneous spaces, while exploring related open problems and conjectures.

In non-commutative space-time deformations, the definition of identical particles breaks down. These models are described by non-abelian space-time symmetries represented by a four-dimensional configuration space. Our approach relies on building the state space from combinations of non-commutative wave functions, allowing us to develop an alternative concept of identity based on particle properties. This leads to the identification of two distinct categories of particles: bosons, characterized by wave functions that remain unchanged under the space-time algebra; and fermions, where the opposite ordering results in a minus sign. This distinction is evident in our calculation of the continuous spectrum, where the particle number is not conserved, leading to a distinction between bosons and fermions.

We apply the two-photon absorption transient current technique to study
properties in three-dimensional charge transport of nitrogen-deficient
single-crystalline type-IIA diamond. By adjusting the focus of a laser beam
over a 100 x 100 um^2 area, we investigate the charge generated in three
-dimensional space. Our measurements reveal a significant increase in current
link to a specific diamond property and provide insight into charge transport
behaviors in diamond. These findings are further supported by numerical modeling
utilizing the COMSOL software.

Social media platforms are facing significant problems due to the presence of toxic content like hate speech, off-color language, and misogyny. These difficulties have caught the attention of the Natural Language Processing (NLP) community, driving innovative research in the field. In this study, we report on the performance of our models in the inaugural Arabic Misogyny Identification challenge, where we evaluate three models that can learn multiple tasks simultaneously, alongside their individual-task counterparts. Our approach relies on the pre-trained MARBERT language model to analyze text inputs. Our results indicate that the proposed models achieved top-tier outcomes, securing first, second, and third place in both the misogyny identification and classification tasks.

This study centres around the solvability of a distinct class of fractional backward stochastic differential equations that take into account past influences within their generators, under Lipschitz condition it's demonstrated that the existence and uniqueness of such equations are assured. Furthermore, a key comparison theorem has been formulated.

We examine if controllers obtained using model-based Reinforcement Learning, which employs an environment model to find the optimal policy, remain robust and adaptable when dealing with slight environmental variations. Building upon the concept from PILCO, a method for probabilistic policy search, our research demonstrates that constraining the uncertainty in the Gaussian Process model's dynamics has a beneficial effect on policy updates and results in more resilient controllers. In addition, our findings highlight the practical advantages of this approach in a simulation-based evaluation.

Several key network communication challenges such as caching and computation are interconnected. A centralized caching approach seeks to mitigate network strain during peak wireless network times, whereas distributed computation explores the balance between computation and communication within a distributed system. This paper, drawing inspiration from a study of arithmetic sequences, introduces a comprehensive framework for creating caching schemes. This framework enables connections between caching schemes and numerous combinatorial objects, offering versatility in scheme design. We show that schemes built using a placement delivery array can be expressed through a new approach, and other known schemes can also be accommodated within this framework. Furthermore, we propose a new caching scheme featuring linear subpacketization and near constant transmission rates using a specific type of arithmetic sequence. Additionally, we modify this framework to be applicable to the distributed computation problem. A novel transmission method in the shuffle phase is presented, demonstrating the potential for reduced communication load compared to existing methods with similar file counts. Furthermore, we present a new computation scheme featuring linear file counts and near constant transmission rates.

We establish a formalization of the Scott model in univalent type theory, adopting a constructive and predicative framework. To capture the essence of non-terminating processes in PCF, we employ the lifting monad from topos theory, which has been adapted for univalent type theory by Escard\'o and Knapp. Our work confirms that using the lifting monad provides a viable way to handle partiality within univalent type theory, and we also demonstrate that a predicative and constructive Scott model is achievable. Notably, we avoid reliance on choice or quotient inductive-inductive types, unlike other approaches to dealing with partiality.

Hanzer and Muić's work on degenerate Eisenstein series cancellations has been built upon, 
extending their method and outcome to a specific set of Eisenstein series, 
specifically those formed from the combinations of two Speh representations 
$\Delta(\tau,m)|\cdot|^{s_1}\otimes\Delta(\tau,n)|\cdot|^{s_2}$ in $GL(m+n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ for self-dual cuspidal automorphic representation $\tau$.

Designing effective collision avoidance systems for mobile robots remains a key challenge, particularly when accounting for the robot's spatial structure.
In this paper, we develop a novel control approach that leverages Control Barrier Functions and Quadratic Programming to enable safe navigation for mobile robotic arms around obstacles, factoring in their unique shape.
Our proposed method successfully incorporates the robot's spatial profile into an optimization framework, allowing it to generate controllable avoidance strategies.
Simulation results for both a simple rod and a modeled robotic arm demonstrate the method's ability to produce efficient collision avoidance trajectories.

Natural language processing, a crucial field of study, strives to comprehend text via digital analysis, despite the inherent imperfections arising from diverse forms of written and spoken language. This work delves into employing various graph-based methodologies for resolving the challenge of text summarization via a selective extraction technique. Two key indicators – sentence overlap and edit distance – are employed for gauging sentence similarity.

Researchers have suggested the application of quantum interferometry and information processing in Bose-Einstein condensates. However, the current understanding of BECs relies on complex descriptions, often through quantum field theory or nonlinear differential equations. These descriptions sometimes conflict with key principles in interferometry and information processing. Nevertheless, a possibility of compatibility remains, and we provide a solid foundation for quantum operations, derived from solving evolution equations, and build upon this base with control techniques and efficient state sampling methods to develop practical nonlinear gates, especially a nonlinear Hadamard gate. Furthermore, our work in BEC interferometry and quantum computing redefines the paradigm by incorporating principles from nonlinear quantum mechanics, effectively applying it to interferometry and information processing.

This paper aims to accomplish two distinct objectives. Firstly, it seeks to establish a unicity theorem for meromorphic mappings from a complete Kähler manifold to a complex projective space, under the constraint of limited intersection with hypersurfaces. Secondly, the paper aims to prove a unicity theorem for the case of nondegenerate meromorphic mappings that share a specified number of hyperplanes in a particular geometric configuration.

Polynomial system solving plays a crucial role in various applications to capture nonlinear geometric attributes. To obtain a solution set devoid of degeneration, which end-users seek to avoid, the nondegenerate locus of a polynomial system needs to be computed. The nondegenerate locus comprises points where the codimension of the solution set matches the number of equations in the system. Historically, the nondegenerate locus has been obtained using ideal-theoretic techniques like saturation ideals and equidimensional decompositions. We propose an algorithm leveraging signature-based features of Gröbner basis algorithms to directly calculate the Gröbner basis for the nondegenerate locus closure without initially solving the entire polynomial system through Gröbner basis computation.

Direct photons have been measured at $p_T<5$ GeV/$c$ for midrapidity and most central events of Cu$+$Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{_{NN}}}=200$ GeV. By calculating the $e^{+}e^{-}$ excess in the $e^{+}e^{-}$ mass distribution over hadronic contributions, we found that quasi-real direct virtual photons dominate the photon spectrum. This is consistent with calculations by the PHENIX Collaboration's transport and photon rate codes, suggesting that the photon spectrum is largely shaped by photon production in the binary collisions and subsequent hadronic interactions. Furthermore, the apparent difference in the $e^{+}e^{-}$ mass spectrum between Cu$+$Cu and Au$+$Au collisions at the same energy may indicate a reduced direct photon yield in Cu$+$Cu collisions due to suppressed cold nuclear matter effects.

The Turan tetrahedron problem seeks to calculate the Turan density of the tetrahedron graph K4^3 by finding the maximum l1-norm of a K4^3-free n-vertex 3-uniform hypergraph's codegree vector. We develop a new method for determining hypergraph extremality and apply it to calculate the asymptotic extremal function of the tetrahedron graph under our novel framework. The codegree squared sum, or co2(G), is introduced to measure codegree magnitude in a 3-uniform hypergraph, with exco2(n,H) representing the maximal codegree squared sum among n-vertex H-free hypergraphs. Utilizing flag algebra computations, we determine the codegree squared extremal numbers for K4^3 and K5^3 and demonstrate associated stability properties, revealing the structural resemblance of extremal K4^3-free hypergraphs to the conjectured extremal hypergraphs of Turan's tetrahedron problem. Additionally, we identify key general characteristics of exco2(n,H), such as the existence of a minimal exponential threshold and the potential for category two extremal hypergraphs.

Achieving a seamless visual experience and optimal system performance when displaying line joins on vector maps requires an efficient anti-aliasing technique. However, the limitations of OpenGL API hinder optimal rendering results when approximating the anti-aliased effect through multiple triangles. In an attempt to rectify this issue, this study introduces a straightforward yet high-performance algorithm utilizing two triangles to replicate fan-shaped line joins via alpha operation. Our findings indicate this technique yields a genuine anti-aliasing effect while reducing memory consumption, raising frame rates, and preventing overlap rendering in map visualization. Our novel anti-aliasing method has been applied in notable applications such as Tencent Mobile Maps and Tencent Automotive Maps.

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. It has been mathematically proven that the modified operator converges at a rate of O(h^2), enabling efficient interpolation of unsmooth functions. Several numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the performance of this new operator.

Pulsar halos are large-scale, high-energy emission structures, formed when energetic electrons and positrons break free from pulsar wind nebulae. As a novel category of gamma-ray emitters, pulsar halos serve as optimal probes for examining the diffusion of cosmic rays within the Galaxy's localized areas, as well as their escape from pulsar wind nebulae. Research on pulsar halos has brought to light that their associated diffusion coefficient is substantially lower than the overall average in the Galaxy, thus generating considerable interest among scientists. We delve into the recent breakthroughs in the study of pulsar halos, including the distinct properties of these sources, identified pulsar halos, theoretical mechanisms underlying their exceptionally slow diffusion, their pivotal roles in investigating cosmic-ray propagation and particle injection, and the implications on the puzzles of excess positrons and the widespread TeV gamma-ray excess. Lastly, we outline the prospective research avenues based on the anticipation of discovering more pulsar halos and carrying out deeper investigations into the brightest sources.

Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse environments and conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the need for a substantial dataset to train effective models.
Existing research has not fully addressed this challenge despite the importance of the application.
To fill this gap, this study contributes a new dataset known as the Multi-Source Weather Classification Dataset (MSWCD), which comprises 102,000 images across six weather categories and utilizes annotated labels for training and evaluation purposes.
Furthermore, to mitigate the data scarcity problem and improve model performance, a novel data augmentation approach is introduced by leveraging radar and satellite weather imagery.
The MSWCD dataset and corresponding code were made available on GitHub for public access to facilitate future research and developments.

Our analysis examines how climate change interest shifts among diverse groups and how their individual interests interconnect. Initially, we track the individual trends, followed by developing a cross-influence model that we then validate using a VAR model. Our results indicate significant fluctuations in the general public's climate change interest, as evident from our creation of a Climate Change Index for Europe and the US based on media mentions, whereas economists show relatively little interest as measured by prominent journal publications. Interestingly, science journals and policymakers display more consistent interest in the past ten years. A notable finding is that policy-related mentions and media mentions exhibit a strong correlation, suggesting a significant increase in G7 policymakers's interest in climate change during Bush's presidency but a significant decline during Trump's presidency. Conversely, economic interest, measured through prominent journal publications, shows no clear correlation with political factors.

Soft grippers are increasingly popular across various applications due to their versatility and flexibility, yet accurately modeling and controlling them to grasp objects efficiently remains challenging. Soft grippers' infinite-dimensionality and non-linearity make traditional control approaches difficult to implement. In response, researchers have turned to data-driven methods. However, current methods typically require extensive model learning through simulations or offline processes, which often fails to adapt to novel scenarios or real-time physical robot control. In response to these limitations, a new method has been developed, employing the Koopman operator theory to map the state space of soft robotic systems. Through online learning and exploitation, this approach achieves self-adaptive model construction and control without the need for prior knowledge or dimension reduction. Resulting trajectories reveal successful grasping and manipulation of various objects, comparing favorably to state-of-the-art contour-actuated soft grippers in terms of performance. In addition, a proposed multi-fingered online learning approach allows for the expansion of existing controllers to handle more complex tasks, enabling a five-fingered robotic hand to learn and grasp objects successfully.

One of the fundamental problems in science and engineering involves finding the lowest cost value for a given function, known as an optimization problem. Various numerical methods have been proposed to solve this problem, but the Gradient Descent method remains the most popular due to its ease and effectiveness. Nonetheless, this approach faces challenges with local minima and slow convergence, particularly when near the optimal point. In response, researchers developed the Natural Gradient Descent method to improve performance across multiple domains, including machine learning, tensor networks, and quantum algorithms. Our work presents a new method to further expand upon NGD, utilizing a suitable reference manifold to expedite convergence and enhance understanding of optimization methods.

High-energy emissions from ancient supermassive black holes can provide a direct look into the black hole activity in the early universe. Specifically, misaligned jets of high-redshift active galaxies should make up a significant portion of these distant galaxy populations. This study uses a highly detailed analysis of data collected from multiple observations of a particularly old and distant galaxy called J2102+6015. High-resolution imaging of J2102+6015's energy emissions, which were captured through a highly precise technique called VLBI at a wavelength of 8.4 GHz, revealed two distinct energy-producing regions. This is in contrast to earlier findings that only detected a single region. Furthermore, the separate areas of energy production show clear movement indicators of a binary system. Given that J2102+6015 is a relatively young and dense galaxy, its measured size and energy output can be explained by a young radio source that is still gaining power. Spectral analyses of J2102+6015's energy emissions reveal that its energy spectrum can be explained by a young radio source that is less than 100 million years old. This discovery is further supported by findings of a relatively high energy output and dense energy production in J2102+6015. Ultimately, this study adds a new entry to a significant collection of verified and ancient supermassive black holes called the 3PERS catalogue.

This research focuses on improving survival time prediction for lung cancer patients, which, despite significant progress in recent years, still lacks effective methods. Current models, both traditional and deep learning-based, primarily rely on single-textual sources such as patient demographics and clinical history. Unlike existing approaches, this study explores the potential of combining multiple data types like text-based clinical information and visual medical scans to inform survival time predictions, simulating the decision-making process of a medical professional. Building on this insight, this work introduces the Lite-ProSENet model, which integrates multiple data modalities and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, yielding an unprecedented 89.3% concordance in predictive accuracy using a dataset from 422 non-small cell lung cancer patients.

A well-designed state representation is crucial in the learning process of Reinforcement Learning. Natural language can be utilized in numerous tasks to either represent the state or constitute it entirely. This overview focuses on the techniques employed by researchers to create natural language state representations, underscoring the need for more transparent and contextualized models, thorough justification of design choices and assessments of the relative effectiveness of varying methodologies.

A novel approach combining machine learning is introduced, enabling the accurate reconstruction of high-redshift cosmological density perturbations through observed quasar spectra analysis. By leveraging sophisticated simulations of cosmic structure formation, a substantial synthetic dataset of absorption spectra and associated 1D matter densities is generated. With this dataset, a series of machine learning models are constructed to predict matter density power spectra. We achieve reconstruction accuracy of approximately 1% for certain wavelengths while noting a corresponding error increase at higher wavelengths. Furthermore, we investigate the size of datasets required to attain a specified error rate, highlighting the data requirements for a desired level of accuracy. This work lays the groundwork for analyzing the forthcoming large-scale datasets anticipated with future observational facilities.

This paper examines certain types of non-weight modules connected to Lie algebras of the Weyl type. Firstly, we establish the characteristics of modules whose restrictions to $U(\frak h)$ are one-dimensional. Next, we identify the requirements for the Lie algebra to support the existence of such modules. Additionally, we explore the relationship between modules of this type and the ideal extensions of the Lie algebras of differential operators.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset.

Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints to open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to consistently
maintain assigned roles during human conversations. Achieving this involves
defining a role specification with specific criteria for stated features and
policies on allowed types of utterances. To build this system, we collect a
dataset of human annotations from existing open-domain dialogue datasets,
annotating them to reflect various role specifications. To demonstrate the
effectiveness of our system building approach, we conduct experiments on a
dataset of role-specific human conversations, showing through an automatic
evaluation that our model excels at upholding these roles in comparison to
unconstrained variants of the model.

The binary black hole merger's aftermath leaves a lasting mark on space-time known as gravitational wave memory, and multiple events create a background of residual disturbance known as the stochastic gravitational wave memory background (SGWMB). Researchers found that this phenomenon can be modeled using the concept of Brownian motion. The strength and distribution of SGWMB are directly tied to the frequency and occurrence rate of binary black hole coalescences, and its power spectral density is primarily determined by the intrinsic properties of these events. Unlike the more common gravitational wave background produced by binary black holes, SGWMB offers a unique window into the accretion history of supermassive black holes due to its ability to be generated by events of virtually any frequency. Furthermore, SGWMB can be distinguished from other gravitational waves through its non-Gaussian characteristics, and its full characterization requires more advanced statistical analysis. Future observations may be able to detect SGWMB using highly sensitive gravitational wave detectors, and the most promising scenario involves the operation of three generations of gravitational wave detectors, beginning with the current generation, including the upcoming KAGRA detector, which covers the spectral range from 2 Hz to 200 Hz.

A hypothetical supersymmetry framework offers an explanation for why large particles weren't discovered by the Large Hadron Collider; this framework predicts the universe underwent a phase transition around the time of the universe's birth that may create ripples in space time that scientists could detect. Developing a realistic model based on how this supersymmetry is broken, researchers found this phase transition can lead to masses in certain heavy particles that may create more particles and a new theory of neutrino mass, as well as ripples in space time that may signal the universe's birth. The same model can help predict signs of these early ripples in space time that may signal the universe's birth. The universe's phase transition can potentially create tiny, extremely dense regions known as black holes that may act as powerful particle smelters.

A reliable and efficient communication system known as semantic communication aims to minimize data transfer and ensure seamless connectivity to diverse users and services. A novel approach to this challenge is presented, incorporating an emergent signaling game framework with a neuro-symbolic artificial intelligence system that facilitates causal reasoning. To design a context-specific communication language, an alternating maximization algorithm optimizes utility values between communication nodes. This language enhances semantic communication by clarifying data transfer and reducing errors. Furthermore, the neuro-symbolic system in this framework improves robustness against errors and uncertainties by utilizing symbolic representations of data. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the proposed system can effectively manage complex data transfer requests, optimize data transfer, and prevent data corruption.

The Natural Language Processing area has garnered disproportionate interest from researchers in the past. A primary factor driving this attention lies in the word prediction challenge, where given a sequence of words in a sentence, a model is tasked with recommending the subsequent word. Researchers have addressed this issue through various techniques, combining either syntactic or semantic analysis methods in the past. However, individually, these approaches often fail to yield practical results in real-world applications. For instance, latent semantic models can capture semantic text characteristics, yet struggle to understand syntactic structures, while syntactic models may learn to generate word sequences based on context, yet often disregard the meaning of words. Consequently, multiple models are combined in hybrid designs in an attempt to cover all aspects of word prediction. This study proposes a hybrid word prediction model, consisting of two main components: the Naive Bayes classifier, which leverages context information to generate word sequences, and a support vector machine, used in conjunction with hand-crafted features to complement the model's output. The integration of these two modules in a hybrid system demonstrates substantial improvements in accuracy, as evidenced by a significant boost in performance on the test dataset, thereby validating the model's effectiveness.

Recent advancements in Session-based recommendation systems have gained popularity for providing personalized, real-time suggestions with high recall rates compared to conventional techniques. Recent examples include STAMP and NARM models, which, however, did not perform as expected on Zalando's Fashion-Similar dataset in comparison to a basic collaborative-filtering method. Our proposed strategy targets improving item ranking by leveraging the encoded session information through an attention network and demonstrates the potential through Candidate Rank Embedding in re-ranking. Experimental results demonstrate a considerable enhancement over the baseline on metrics such as Recall, MRR, and Click-Through-Rate in an online setting, and we further observed improvements when applied to STAMP and NARM models on two public real-world datasets for the task of next-click prediction.

We examine a rigid structure composed of two active Brownian particles that interact in an activity gradient. We demonstrate analytically that the position of the dimer varies based on the angle between the particles and accumulates either at areas with high activity levels or low activity levels. This corresponds to chemotaxis and antichemotaxis respectively. Some dimer configurations display chemotactic and antichemotactic properties, with their behavior determined by the activity gradient strength. A coarsely detailed approach helps to generate an effective potential, used in our analysis to create a phase diagram. This diagram classifies dimer configurations based on their tactic behavior and also indicates how some dimers can maintain direction and achieve greater persistence in motion. This study provides valuable insights into the design of autonomous, responsive colloidal systems that can navigate according to varying activity levels in their environment.

A thorough approach is outlined to simulate single-phase flow in fractured porous media. The proposed methodology comprises three core components: generating an accurate 3D mesh of a fracture network, solving governing equations using a high-order numerical method, and implementing high-performance computing techniques. A mesh generation strategy that handles problematic cases to maintain high mesh quality is presented. A versatile simulator utilizes process kernels to enable flexible interactions between the fracture and matrix domains. We validate the model through comparison with known analytical solutions and by examining numerical convergence in different scenarios. Two case studies are presented: the first investigates how fractures can impact flow in different configurations, and the second explores flow and transport through a large cubic domain with randomly distributed fractures.

This study centers on low-energy collision avoidance and maintenance of autonomous drone swarms. Two key issues arise in achieving these goals: firstly, determining optimal strategies to temporarily disband the formation to avoid collisions (collision avoidance reformation), and secondly, effecting this reformation while minimizing the time and energy spent by the drones. To resolve the first challenge, a cellular automata-based method is utilized to identify efficient formations that evade obstacles while reducing time and energy consumption. To tackle the second issue, a near-optimal reformation strategy after successful collision avoidance is realized through a temperature function reduction technique borrowed from the point set registration process. The objective of this reformation process is to rapidly eliminate disturbances, thus minimizing the time required for the swarm to reach its destination and ultimately lowering the energy consumption of this process. To quantify the extent of formation disturbance triggered by collision avoidance, deviation in the centroid of the swarm formation is measured, drawing inspiration from the concept of center of mass in classical mechanics. The study's experimental outcomes validate the efficacy of the proposed technique in terms of performance and energy efficiency.

This research explores various spectral characteristics of the Seidel matrix associated with a connected chain graph, demonstrating that $-1$ is always an eigenvalue, while other eigenvalues may have a multiplicity of at most two. We derive the multiplicity of the eigenvalue $-1$, the minimum number of unique eigenvalues, eigenvalue limits, the characteristic polynomial, and bounds for the Seidel energy of a chain graph, which outperform previously proposed energy bounds by Haemers. We also obtain the minimum Seidel energy for specific chain graphs of order $n$, along with presenting several unresolved questions.

In our investigation, we focus on a mean-field optimal control issue for stochastic differential equations featuring time-delay, which are influenced by fractional Brownian motion with a Hurst parameter exceeding 0.5. Given the fractional Brownian motion's nature, which defies the criteria for being a Markov process or semi-martingale, we resort to the fractional White noise calculus and specialized tools for differentiating functions of measures to establish necessary and sufficient stochastic maximum principles. This approach is further exemplified by two applications, including solving a delayed consumption optimization problem from a cash flow and a linear-quadratic problem under delay constraints.

We've developed a unique, detailed two-parameter set of finite-band Jacobi elliptic potentials that correspond to the non-self-adjoint Dirac operator, seamlessly linking two well-known limit cases, each associated with the absence or presence of elliptic parameters. To thoroughly analyze the Dirac operator's spectrum, we've made connections between periodic/antiperiodic eigenvalue problems for the operator, equivalent tridiagonal operator actions in weighted Hilbert spaces and relevant Heun equation connection issues. This, in turn, ties into four related non-self-adjoint, unbounded tridiagonal operator eigenvalue problems which surprisingly possess real eigenvalues.

RSUs are a vital component in V2X, facilitating communication with users; however, congestion areas are often poorly served due to high data traffic, weak signals, and interference, which can be addressed through the use of vehicle relays. To enhance the network in these situations, this research utilizes stochastic geometry to develop an innovative analytical framework for the performance evaluation of vehicular networks incorporating RSUs, vehicle relays, and mobile vehicle users. Our two-dimensional analytical model effectively considers the interplay between RSUs, vehicle relays, and vehicle users within the same plane, and validates the accuracy of the developed method through comparisons with simulation results, showcasing its precision in predicting performance outcomes and highlighting the benefits of using vehicle relays to mitigate coverage blind spots and improve data transfer speeds in high-data-volume applications.

Wikipedia's ultimate goal is to be an authoritative reference on various topics.  However, due to a limited number of editors and a vast amount of articles, only 0.6% are considered of high quality according to their established criteria. To enhance article quality through machine learning, we must first label individual sentences as high or low quality, yet this process relies on human annotations that are time-consuming and often yield inaccuracies. To resolve this, we developed an automated method for marking article quality by analyzing semantic modifications in French and German Wikipedia articles, demonstrating a 10% improvement in accuracy over existing, supervised machine learning models. Furthermore, we discovered that edit patterns can generate over 800 new labels, outperforming the existing Wikipedia-based features that rely on textual data.

Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible. A series of experiments using multiple architecures and datasets demonstrate the efficacy of this approach.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The branching fractions for these decays are calculated as follows: The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (4.3±0.5±0.3±0.3±0.6) ×10^-4, and the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (2.8±1.0±0.3±0.2±0.4) ×10^-4, with the given uncertainties stemming from various sources.

The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality developed by Mathai and Rosenberg is applied to a broad class of topological spaces encompassing torus bundles, nilmanifolds, and other examples from string theory. By constructing T-duals from commutative $C^*$-algebras with ${\mathbb R}^n$ action, we establish a simple method for achieving this transformation. Our work rigorously addresses almost abelian solvmanifolds across arbitrary dimensions, offering both left and right actions, and we relate the classical T-duals of compact solvmanifolds to the real spectrum of the reduced twisted spectral radius. Furthermore, we provide detailed case studies for two-dimensional solvmanifolds, offering geometric interpretations of the developed algebraic framework.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by selecting training objectives that promote both collaborative and competitive learning. As a result, agents not only gain from each other's successes but also learn from their failures. Empirical evidence suggests that CoIL effectively facilitates the exchange of information, enabling agents to learn more efficiently and more effectively, even in the absence of expert input.

This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes with the proposed metric function. We show that using the polarized cutoff rate as the bias in our metric function reduces the risk of incorrect path selection during decoding, exponentially decreasing as the incorrect path depth increases. We also prove and validate the Pareto distribution of PAC code computation complexity. Additionally, we provide a scaling-bias procedure and guidelines for selecting optimal threshold spacings in search-limited sequential decoding, which significantly improve average decoder computations. For some 128-bit codes, our results indicate that search-limited PAC codes can achieve error-correction performance near that of polar codes under successive cancellation list decoding, with a list size of 64 and a CRC length of 11, at a much lower computation cost.

This project tackles the complex problem of simultaneously monitoring the positions and shapes of hands and objects in a sequence of depth point cloud data, starting from the known poses in the initial frame. To achieve this, we introduce a network called HandTrackNet, the first point cloud-based hand joint tracking system, to calculate hand joint movement between frames. Our novel hand pose canonicalization module simplifies this task and enables accurate tracking of hand joints. By converting these joints into a template-based hand model called MANO, our system can reconstruct the entire hand. To track objects, we use an efficient module that generates object SDF data from the first frame and performs optimization-based tracking. Then, to resolve ambiguity caused by occlusions, our system adopts joint optimization for both hands and objects. In our training process, our system only uses simulated, highly variable synthetic data for ease of generalization, making our system more versatile. Our method performs well on real in-the-wild hand-object interaction datasets such as HO3D and DexYCB and uncovers novel interactions not detected by human observers.

This study employs the modular reduction technique to a Coxeter group of rank 4 featuring a star diagram with 5, 3, and k= 3, 4, 5, or 6 labels, using the odd primes from the ring Z[tau], where tau represents the golden ratio. It categorizes each reduced group as spherical or affine, and also provides symbols for their associated Satake diagrams.

A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically develop and utilize real-world models for identifying and positioning the end-effector, predicting object rotation, and pinpointing critical points in a single image frame. A mathematical transformation and a keypoint-matching algorithm allow us to accurately estimate end-effector pose based on rotation and keypoint data. Enhanced system robustness is achieved through a combination of advanced algorithms, including iterative keypoint refinement, multi-frame processing, and the utilization of local features, diverse data sets, and real-time depth data. Results demonstrate the superiority of our method over previous techniques in terms of accuracy and processing speed.

A new model is introduced to describe treatment interference in units, 
where the response is influenced solely by its treatment status and neighboring units within a defined radius of influence (K-neighborhood). Traditional approaches for identifying interference involve controlled randomized trials and statistical tests focused on specific, selected units (focal units). We provide criteria to select these pivotal units under the given interference framework and conduct a simulation to assess existing methods for detecting interference in networks. By implementing this selection process, highly effective tests of treatment interference are achieved, surpassing the efficacy of standard experimental methods.

Calculations of neutrino emissions from self-destructing dark matter particles within a star are being conducted. In the core of a star that has not yet undergone nuclear reactions, it's observed that the interactions between these particles and the star's constituent atoms via a particular particle can produce an unusually large number of neutrinos, which may equal and potentially surpass those produced by the star's nuclear reactions early on. This process primarily involves two reactions: a collision of two dark matter particles resulting in neutrinos or intermediate particles that then decay into neutrinos, which may be confined to less than 1-2 percent of the star's volume and persist throughout the star's lifetime. This information is then used to refine estimates of the impact of dark matter particle collisions on the cooling of a star in the early stages of a star's formation.

The ongoing UNIONS project, the most comprehensive optical survey to date in the Northern sky, has partnered with CFIS for $r$-band data collection, boasting exceptional seeing of 0.65 arcseconds and complete magnitude 24.5 for precise weak-lensing research. Our analysis covers an expansive 1700 square degrees of the sky, cataloging 40 million galaxies, translating to a density of 6.8 per square arcminute. A low-level systematic bias was found in this research, providing a groundwork for extensive cosmological studies when the full 4800 square degree survey is completed. Introducing ShapePipe, a cutting-edge pipeline leveraging Ngmix for precise galaxy shape detection and metacalibration for accurate shear calibration, the study extensively validates the pipeline through Point Spread Function, galaxy shape tests, and realistic simulations, confirming minimal systematics. Analyzing the shear two-point correlation function reveals a low-level systematics influence compared to cosmological contribution. Shear bias was found to be under 5 times 10^-4 and up to 10^-3 in residual multiplicative bias, confirming the efficacy of the pipeline. Using COSEBIs, no significant B-modes are detected in second-order shear statistics, displaying pronounced correlations between E-modes and known clusters, as well as E-modes that decline with increasing depth.

A notable consequence of a finding made by Veech more than 50 years ago, relating to the mod $2$ form of the Kronecker-Weyl theorem, has to do with sequences of irrational rotations of the form $\{q\alpha\}$. In the event that a certain number $\alpha$ resists being closely approximated by rational numbers and another number $b$ in the interval $(0,1)$ differs from the rotation sequence for no integer $m$, then, as $N$ approaches infinity, the parity of the sizes of sets consisting of numbers of the form $\{q\alpha\}$ within the interval $[0,b)$ that correspond to $q$ values up to $N$ displays evenly distributed occurrences.

The text also discusses how it answers a query put forth by Veech, thereby providing a revised mod $n$ form of a prior result (as stated in Theorem 3.1). A characterization, based on specific values, of scenarios where evenly distributed occurrences result (especially when $b$ equals the rotation sequence for some natural number $m$ and $\alpha$ is an irrational number) is also proposed (as stated in Theorem 2.1). A time-quantitative description, which is rooted in Ostrowski and $\alpha$-expansion representations, of certain cases of violations to uniformity, which is a highly number theoretic area, has also been discovered (as stated in Theorem

We prove that for k-rational singularities of local complete intersections, k-Du Bois classification applies. For hypersurfaces, k-rationality can be determined based on the minimal exponent. Moreover, certain local vanishing properties for k-rational and k-Du Bois singularities have been identified. These properties were also discovered separately by [FL2].

We've observed the appearance of field-induced Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless correlations in a weakly coupled, spin-1/2 Heisenberg material called [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2. Due to its moderate exchange coupling of about 6.8 Kelvin, the application of laboratory magnetic fields produces a noticeable anisotropy of the spin correlations in an XY plane. This significant BKT regime develops because of a weak interlayer exchange of about one millikelvin that causes 3D correlations as the critical temperature is approached, resulting in an exponential increase in spin-correlation length. Nuclear magnetic resonance, muon spin resonance measurements and quantum Monte Carlo simulations using the experimentally determined parameters are employed to determine the critical temperatures associated with BKT transitions as well as long-range order. Finite-size scaling of the spin stiffness based on our in-plane theory shows a perfect match between theoretical and experimental critical temperatures, clearly indicating that the complex magnetic phase diagram of [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2 is determined by field-induced XY anisotropy and concomitant BKT physics.

Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. In doing so, it also resolves issues with strong CP problems and stabilizes the electroweak vacuum while fitting within observational limits of Higgs inflation. The resulting model, referred to as the axion-stere neutrino model, has a comprehensive set of criteria that makes it robust and versatile. The incorporation of a Sterile Neutrino adds an extra layer of reliability as it makes the neutrino sector more straightforward, with the potential cost of violating lepton number symmetry, $\mathbb{Z}_{11}$, which is heavy and thus not able to influence low-energy processes. The model, with the exception of the neutrino sector, has gapped symmetries that make it suitable for natural particle physics. The Sterile Neutrino's mass, in this model, is within reach of future collider experiments. The extensive review of the axion-stere neutrino model's capabilities provides solid evidence in support of this model as a reliable and reliable theory of nature.

This study optimizes the execution time of established algorithms for classically simulating quantum circuits comprising Clifford and T gates. The efficiency improvement stems from deriving a novel upper limit for the number of stabilizer states required to express $m$ copies of the magic state, $|T\rangle$. The findings reveal that a superposition of no more than $O(2^{\alpha m})$ stabilizer states can accurately represent $|T\rangle^{\otimes m}$, where $\alpha\leq 0.3963$. This surpasses the earlier upper limit of $\exp(\frac{\log 3}{\log 2}m+\sqrt{m\ln 2})$ and yields significant time savings in classically simulating quantum circuits involving multiple T gates. As a related achievement, we have also determined that a superposition of no more than $O(2^{\beta m})$ stabilizer states is needed to express $|T\rangle^{\otimes m}$ for any state $|T\rangle$ obtained through Clifford+T evolution, with $\beta\leq0.4168, and showed that this is the optimal exponent achievable with near-optimal error margins of $\pm\eta$, with $\eta$ not exceeding $2^{-\gamma m}$, where $\gamma\leq 0.1596. This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy model in two scenarios, 
non-interacting and interacting, to calculate essential parameters for the energy 
density equation of state within the FRW universe, analogous to a quintessence model.
We will determine the scaling scalar field, scalar field potential, and derive 
scalar field dynamics in both scenarios, followed by assessing cosmological 
constraints on the model parameters by utilizing the Hubble data sets.
Notably, our analysis reveals that the Tsallis model surpasses the general 
quintessence model in explaining the current universe's state, as evidenced by 
lower AIC and BIC values.

Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using four $K$2 plates. This study, which involved low- and medium-resolution spectroscopic surveys, gathered a significant amount of data. The low-resolution spectroscopic survey yielded around 767,000 spectra after 25 nights of 46.6 hours of exposures and a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 70% of its spectra. The medium-resolution spectroscopic survey took 177 exposures and around 49.1 hours over 27 nights to collect around 478,000 spectra. The data showed a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 50% of its spectra. To estimate the stellar parameters and radial velocities, the LAMOST research team utilized several different methods such as LASP, DD-Payne, and SLAM. These estimations demonstrated good agreement and were consistent with those of the APOGEE study. By analyzing the $Gaia$ DR2 data, the LAMOST research team corrected for radial velocity zero points on a per exposure basis, showing good alignment with the APOGEE study. To estimate stellar masses, the LAMOST research team utilized stellar parameters and multi-band magnitudes in combination with distances and extinction values.
