This paper explores the recovery of one-dimensional Radon measures on a torus from their low-frequency Fourier components, which are defined as the first N=|Z_+^s (s>0 and N an integer) Fourier modes with the highest amplitude. The proposed method, variants of which were initially introduced by Candes, Ren, Carlier and O'Connell in 2016, can recover such measures with precision up to a frequency of order N^-(1+ε) (with ε>0 and extremely small) even in the presence of arbitrarily high levels of noise. With the introduction of new techniques, we're now able to prove that the solution, which is the recovery process, is not only reliable but also uniquely correct for values of N much higher than our previous estimate of order N^-(1/3), with the lower bound improving to order N^-(1/2). The same techniques allow us to prove that the solution is not only reliable but also uniquely correct for values of s much higher than our previous estimate of order s=1/4, with the lower bound improving to order s=1/2.

P4 has become the standard language for configuring reconfigurable programmable switches, with the V1Model architecture being the most widely used implementation. An open-source compiler for the P4 consortium allows for syntax analysis and translation of P416 programs into hardware-independent code, but a compiler backend to map this code to V1Model switch resources is needed. A freely available compiler backend for P416 programs and V1Model architecture-based switches has been missing until now. Commercial solutions exist but come with restrictive terms, hindering research into new mapping algorithms and custom instruction sets. Our work fills this gap with an open-source compiler backend for the V1Model architecture, utilizing heuristic-based mapping algorithms to optimize P416 programs for different hardware resources. This allows rapid prototyping of different mapping approaches and provides resource usage metrics for comparison.

In numerical simulations involving fluid dynamics, the Raviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables such as velocity or momentum on a quadrilateral mesh. Nevertheless, the standard discretisation of the vector transport equation has a notable error limitation, which is only one order higher than the standard method. To overcome this restriction, two methods have been developed to improve the accuracy of the vector transport equation. Firstly, a post-processing approach will be presented which achieves optimal levels of accuracy without introducing additional variables. Secondly, a modified method of lines will be discussed which also reaches optimal levels of accuracy but does allow the introduction of additional variables. Both schemes have been designed to be adaptable for use with a wide range of quadrilateral meshes and have been demonstrated to work effectively in a number of numerical examples.

The remarkable performance of deep neural networks in addressing real-world issues has led to a widespread adoption in both private and public sectors.  Despite this success, there are ongoing challenges to address several important aspects. The ability of deep learning models to accurately replicate the characteristics of their environment represents both benefits and risks. To this end, researchers have suggested the application of fairness metrics and the implementation of privacy protection mechanisms such as K-center clustering with a differential privacy component as possible solutions.  What if we were to combine all these concepts into a comprehensive framework? This article explores the development of such a framework and evaluates the trade-offs involved in maintaining fairness and implementing differential privacy within the context of federated learning. To this end, we propose a novel approach based on the federated learning k-means algorithm with clustering-based privacy protection and an adaptive fairness metric that can be controlled. We examine the trade-offs involved in maintaining fairness and implementing differential privacy, demonstrate that our approach offers more efficient privacy protection compared to traditional methods, and achieve notable improvements in both privacy and fairness results. The developed framework attains significant reductions in communication overhead and tolerates a certain level of privacy breaches as long as it provides acceptable fairness levels to the users. Notably, we observe that this type of balance is achievable, as we can prioritize either the fairness or privacy concerns of the users and still yield satisfactory results.

Scientists analyzed collision data from the LHCb experiment to identify excited states of a particular subatomic particle, known as the B-c plus. They found two peaks in the data, each corresponding to a possible state. One state has a mass of around 6841.2 MeV and fits expectations for a particular predicted state. A second state has a mass of around 6872.1 MeV and may be consistent with a different predicted state.

In the last few years, the creation of accurate numerical solutions for problems with Hamiltonian dynamics led to the establishment of a specific class of energy-preserving Runge-Kutta methods known as Hamiltonian Boundary Value Methods (HBVMs). These methods can be interpreted as a continuous, multi-step approach, similar to Runge-Kutta methods but with continuous stages, and are explored here in the context of more general differential problems.

This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing specialized networks to refine neural network updates. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and applying error gradients from corresponding critic modules, the learning process is efficiently decoupled for both CNNs and RNNs. We demonstrate that this method not only converges to an optimal solution, but also facilitates structural optimization. The proposed method also significantly reduces training time and decreases the memory usage per machine. The code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/hjdw2/Local-critic-training.

Three-dimensional chaotic scattering has garnered less attention than its two-dimensional counterpart. In this research, a three-dimensional open Hamiltonian system is analyzed where the non-dissipative boundaries initially deviate from Wada's characteristics, changing topologically. Focusing on the effects of dissipation, this study investigates how this system alters when weak dissipation lowers the system's energy below its critical value. Interestingly, this investigation finds that non-Wada basins transition into partially Wada basins under such weak dissipation. Moreover, numerical results demonstrate the emergence of Wada points on the boundaries of these basins in three-dimensional systems. Ultimately, this research indicates that Wada basins in three-dimensional systems exhibit increased stability when subjected to low levels of dissipation.

A theoretical model involving an intricate scalar field that connects to (electron, muon) or (muon, tau) pairs is considered within a certain "duration" window where the mass difference between two lepton types lies between their sum and the absolute difference. Although a moderately large interaction between this scalar field and the two lepton types could lead to extended lifetimes and larger observable distances between their birth and death points. By leveraging existing neutrino experiments and an upcoming one, we plan to explore various possible scenarios of this theoretical model. For instance, the INO experiment has the capability to provide a joint constraint on all relevant parameters in a specific scenario where the interaction between this scalar field and the three generations of leptons varies significantly. This scalar can decay into a muon and an electron or vice versa and given that the muon/electron separation distance is quite large, even a long-lived scalar can traverse considerable space before decaying. Furthermore, we can utilize other lepton decay patterns such as the muon decaying into an electron and a scalar, or the electron decaying into a muon and a scalar, and derive parameters for these scenarios which may be probed by the muon electron separation sensitivity of the HL-LHC. This particular study explores the relationship between this scalar's interaction with two nearby lepton types and its mass, and derives parameters for both individual lepton decay patterns as well as the joint lepton decay pattern in various different windows of 'duration'.

Human action understanding in complex videos has far-reaching applications, 
which can be leveraged through deep learning techniques. Nevertheless, 
classifying human actions within videos remains challenging due to variations 
in human body poses, movements and the challenging conditions often present 
in real-world videos. Our proposed Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN) is 
an advanced model for classifying human actions in videos. HAN is comprised 
of two main components: the Body Pose Feature Extraction module and the video 
classification module. The first component utilizes a body pose estimator to 
generate a comprehensive representation of human body poses, which are then 
processed through a series of hierarchical attention-based neural networks. 
Ultimately, the output represents a refined set of features that capture key 
movement details about the performing subject's actions. Our experimental 
results demonstrate that HAN surpasses the performance of state-of-the-art 
models, achieving exceptional results on several benchmark action 
recognition datasets.

Investigating the thermodynamics and cosmic censorship conjecture in Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes through scalar field scattering yields results that support the first law of thermodynamics for non-extremal black holes, confirming that the singularity in such black holes is hidden by an event horizon. The validity of this theory for near-extremal and extremal black holes is confirmed by demonstrating that the singularity is obscured by an event horizon, with an analysis that includes the maximum extent of the event horizon. The findings also suggest that the weak cosmic censorship conjecture is upheld in Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes.

This article will examine the concept of star formation (SF) through observation, and its progression over time, offering a fresh understanding of the process, particularly relevant since planet formation emerges from it and sheds new light on the origins of life in the universe.

This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate uncertainty metrics, such as cross-entropy and specific entropy, for complex Bayesian models that are intractable to evaluate directly. By leveraging nested sampling, we can bypass the intractability and develop a straightforward algorithm to estimate these metrics at any level of precision. Furthermore, this method enables us to calculate the posterior distribution's entropy, although this requires some additional theoretical framework. To illustrate the proposed approach, we apply it to Bayesian stochastic thermal equilibrium and quantum field theory.

We re-examine a widely accepted model for complex semiconductor production lines and analyze it in the context of states, inflows, and outflows being represented by measures on Borel spaces. This investigation arises from the lack of optimal solutions for transitioning from a smaller to a larger equilibrium state with zero inventory levels in the standard L1 framework. Novel contributions involve addressing the issue of non-differentiable velocities with discrete objects and a bounded domain subject to inflows and outflows. Employing a Lagrangian perspective, we establish that solutions exist and are unique and define a notion of weak solutions. Furthermore, we prove that the flow is continuous with respect to time, and also with respect to the initial condition. However, due to generally non-differentiable velocities, these refined results come at the cost of a 'fanning out' phenomenon in the direction of time, where solutions do not remain compact in the phase space.

Cybersecurity has gained significant importance over recent years, with the detection of cyber threats emerging as a critical task due to the immense damage a single breach can inflict on companies. The incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) into this task has improved it, allowing high-quality classifiers to detect attacks efficiently; however, these classifiers demand substantial computing power or memory. The scenario presents a problem, particularly when these classifiers need to operate on low-resource devices or prevent performance overload on devices with IoT or industrial applications. A novel solution to overcome this challenge is proposed by NBcoded, a light attack classification tool that effectively combines noisy data removal and efficient data encoding, leveraging the benefits of Naive Bayes classifier while reducing resource requirements. In this study, three NBcoded implementations are developed using three Naive Bayes likelihood distribution assumptions (Gaussian, Complement, and Bernoulli). The implementations compare the performance of NBcoded, including its computational and memory requirements to state-of-the-art classifiers, demonstrating that NBcoded outperforms existing classifiers in both areas.

For finitely generated groups G, the focus of this article is the geometric property of growth in graphs representing faithful G-actions. We introduce a concept of Schreier growth gap, a function that measures group growth, by examining its potential gaps when G acts geometrically on a graph. We then explore and classify the Schreier growth gap for solvable groups, demonstrating that it is inherently non-trivial. If G is metabelian, the Schreier growth gap can be related to counting methods from the group's commutator subgroup. For finite groups, the Schreier growth gap equals the growth gap. Additionally, the article presents various examples and counter-examples that highlight its distinct implications for different types of groups.

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, social connections, and escaping predators; thus, analyzing their motion is vital in the fields of biology, ecology, and conservation. This leads to several challenges: evaluating motion plans that account for unpredictable environments, detecting animals without clear visual identifiers, and tracking animals that frequently die and then reappear. An effective method for analyzing animal motion is therefore necessary to tackle these complexities. This paper describes our proposed solution to the wildtrack challenge, which won first place in both the main and lightweight tracks of the competition. Our approach is divided into several distinct phases, starting from image processing to validate the presence of an animal, followed by a machine learning-based classification of locomotion patterns, and ending with a development of a graph-based matching algorithm for tracking animals in motion sequences. A particular challenge arose in our solution due to a discontinuous data set, which made it necessary to employ a pre-processing step for data alignment. Ultimately, our approach successfully detected motion patterns in videos of animals under various conditions.

Maximizing efficient electricity usage across transmission power networks requires optimized surplus management to minimize costs.
In our study, we demonstrated the effectiveness of using quantum annealing for optimizing power networks by defining the QUBO problem and implementing solutions on both purely quantum and hybrid architectures.
The D-Wave hybrid solver and classical solvers on Azure Quantum were utilized to solve the problem, yielding hybrid approaches that outperformed classical methods in solution quality due to lower objective function values, regardless of problem size variations.

Modern artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methods are now employed to automatically identify physics principles and governing equations directly from measurement data. Nevertheless, formulating a universal physical law using data exclusively proves to be difficult without proposing a corresponding discrepancy model to account for the theoretical-measurement discrepancies that inevitably arise. By reexamining the long-standing problem of simulating the falling motions of objects with diverse size and mass, this work highlights several critical issues that need to be resolved by data-driven methods of automated physics discovery. It's particularly demonstrated that noise from measurements and secondary physical mechanisms such as complex drag forces, can mask the law of gravity, thus leading to incorrect model development. Utilizing the SINDy (sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics) method, which involves the use of real-world and simulated trajectory measurements, it's illustrated how the assumption that each object is governed by a similar physical law can increase the stability of learned models, although significant discrepancies between predictions and observations persist, primarily due to the intricacies of drag dynamics. This study's findings serve as a reminder of the inherent challenges in extracting universal physical laws from data and serve as a call to action for the ML and data-driven physics community to develop methods capable of tackling these issues.

This study employs the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider to investigate the presence of hypothetical heavy, charged, long-lived particles in proton-proton collisions amounting to 139 inverse femtobarns of data collected at 13 TeV energy. The search targets particles with significantly lower speeds than light and distinctive characteristics: substantial transverse momentum and unusually large energy loss per unit length. The study compares observed results with predictions based on simulated data for standard model particles and processes, as well as hypothetical signs of long-lived charged particles with lifetimes ranging from 1 cm to 100 km and masses between 100 and 500 GeV. The study focuses on particles unstable under the standard model and capable of fitting within the theoretical framework of the supersymmetric models of charged long-lived particles, particularly the assumption of a 500 GeV $t\bar{t}^{\rm R}$ particle with a 100 km lifetime and 34 GeV mass, which would require an increase in charged particles of at least 15% over the predicted background at a 95% confidence level.

We have developed a numerical approach to maximize coupling efficiency in single-photon sources consisting of a quantum dot-cavity and a ridge waveguide by conducting simulations using the finite element method. A design optimized for a 1D nanobeam cavity yielded a notable source efficiency of 97.7 percent and an impressive Purcell factor of 38.6 for an isotropic dipole, primarily due to a combination of high index contrast between GaAs and SiO$_2$ materials and an effective cavity design that facilitated interference and minimized losses. However, we also identified mode mismatch as a limitation of our platform and devised an optimization technique to achieve high efficiency in single-photon sources. This method incorporates a taper section to smoothly bridge the mode mismatch between the cavity and the nanobeam, ultimately enhancing the Purcell factor and source efficiency. Furthermore, we observed the resilience of our design in the face of real-world fabrication imperfections affecting hole variation. Specifically, we examined the impact of varying hole sizes on the Purcell factor and source efficiency and observed the resilience of our design under different conditions. Furthermore, we observed the isolation of our system from thermal fluctuations and demonstrated the maintenance of high efficiency and Purcell factor even in the presence of significant thermal variations.

Neutron inelastic scattering is a valuable tool that not only allows for the identification of a glass's vibrational modes near its boson peak, but also provides insight into the specific mode itself, including its frequency, helical structure, and spatially localized motion. The boson peak, a unique feature in the density of states of glassy materials, is thought to be associated with a collective or shared vibrational mode that approaches a critical state. By using advanced neutron techniques such as spin-echo spectroscopy and time-of-flight spectroscopy, researchers can study this phenomenon in detail and develop mathematical models that accurately represent the boson peak. The application of different mathematical models to data from various materials, including silicon dioxide and boron oxide, demonstrates the ability to accurately fit and predict the boson peak's behavior in different substances.

Particle physics is becoming increasingly data-driven, driven by the success of the Standard Model and the discoveries at the Large Hadron Collider. However, current computational methods using finite field techniques or symbolically integrating are reaching their limits with complex calculations, such as loop-level amplitudes with multiple loops, scales, and high precision. This has become a critical issue for top-quark-dominated calculations, particularly with the upcoming precision physics demands at the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider. To meet these demands, an advanced mathematical framework is required that can evaluate complex integrals with multiple scales and loops while handling high-precision calculations. This thesis contributes to addressing this challenge by developing a mathematical framework for multi-loop, multi-scale Feynman integrals with arbitrary Breitenberger parameters and evaluates two integrals to all orders using this framework. This solution employs state-of-the-art mathematical techniques, incorporating the Riemann-Hilbert problem and cohomological techniques to simplify complex calculations. This approach is highly versatile, allowing it to be applied to a wide variety of integrals and is independent of any specific behind-the-scenes computational methods. This framework can be applied to solve a wide range of integrals and is expected to significantly contribute to evaluating multi-loop amplitudes in the future.

In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume, and previously this correlation was leveraged to increase energy delivered to a target. This study determines a general set of constraints and formulas governing the eigenvalues and modes within any given scattering setup - including complex geometries, and broad categories such as slabs and narrow channels. Our mathematical framework reveals limitations and correlations for intensity within system boundaries, and derived properties apply universally to different types and strengths of wave, and multiple wave types.

Researchers have identified the far-side counterpart to a well-studied spiral arm in the center of the Milky Way, which is observed expanding. This far-side arm, detected through carbon monoxide emissions, can be followed in a map of Galactic longitude and velocity as a faint feature extending at least 20 degrees. Both the far-side and near-side arms exhibit comparable features including velocities, widths, heights, and mass distribution. Based on further investigation using 21-cm data, it's found that these spiral arms are primarily composed of molecular gas. This new evidence lends support to the presence of a bar structure at the center of the Galaxy and should aid in understanding its properties.

Increasingly, optimization methods are being employed to uncover a broad range of solutions. Our comparison across multi-objective optimization, multimodal optimization, and quality diversity in a straightforward context reveals that multi-objective optimization may not consistently generate significant diversity. By contrast, multimodal optimization tends to yield solutions with superior fitness levels. Meanwhile, quality diversity proves to be resilient to genetic neutrality and yields the most diverse set of solutions overall. Furthermore, integrating an autoencoder allows for the automated discovery of phenotypic features, which, in conjunction with quality diversity, facilitates the creation of a more extensive and diverse solution set. Ultimately, we offer strategic guidance on the appropriate applications of these optimization techniques.

The Stable Roommates problem concerns pairing a set of agents according to their individual preference lists with specific hierarchical rankings. A key condition for any established pairings is that they must remain stable - preventing the situation where two agents would prefer each other over their respective matches. Variants of the Stable Roommates problem, including those involving larger groups of agents and specific capacity limitations at potential matches, have been the subject of comprehensive study. A more complex form of the Stable Roommates problem, adding a level of sophistication to agent preferences through functions that are representable by utilities such as linear or convex, has also been explored. It has been demonstrated that such additively separable preferences introduce significant complexity to the Stable Roommates problem. Our research finds that, in general, finding suitable matchings that satisfy stability is a computationally difficult task. However, specific restrictions on agent preferences and possible matches can make it easier to find stable matchings. Additionally, the difficulty of improving existing matchings that are close to stable, in terms of finding better matches for individual agents and making substitutions locally, is a challenging problem. Even with restricted forms of additively separable preferences, such as linear or convex, it is generally difficult to improve existing matchings. Our findings provide insights into the computational tractability of stable matching problems with additively separable preferences, highlighting the need for further research into general applicability and the potential for approximate solutions.

Our research systematically explores how different mechanisms of electron-phonon
interaction affect valley behavior in two-dimensional materials. When ordinary
electron-phonon coupling occurs, additional valley isolation mechanisms can be
activated due to lattice deformation. Introducing structural irregularities can
lead to a bandgap variation influenced by phonons, thereby creating distinct
valley populations. In cases of significant strain effects on the lattice, the
valley degeneracy can be partially lifted, and if there is a significant impact on
the bandgap, isolated valleys can arise. For extreme cases of distorted lattices,
valley decoupling can be fully achieved. This study provides a comprehensive
analysis of how different electron-phonon interaction mechanisms influence
valley phenomena in two-dimensional materials.

We examine the class of all metric spaces with their distances measured by Gromov--Hausdorff distance. The subsets of spaces with bounded distances are the clouds, whose leaders are the spaces with maximal diameters. A previous result showed that every cloud has a central space, where "central" is defined by a norm-like metric. Here, we prove that every cloud has a central space, where the metric is not necessarily normed. This goal is achieved by proving two other results. First, we demonstrate that the stable unit ball of any Banach space is a central space. Second, we show that the approximation of a metric space by a set of finite representations forms a complete system and that this system has a central space.

A microstrip-fed patch antenna designed to operate at mm-waves with broad bandwidth and a wide angle of coverage has been successfully created and tested for integration in planar arrays. The designed antenna has a significant bandwidth of 13.1%, operating between 34.1 GHz and 38.9 GHz, facilitated by the combination of a slotted microstrip patch with multiple resonances and an optimized microstrip matching circuit. Constructed using the low-cost RO3003 substrate with top and ground layers, this design accommodates simple integration with other microstrip and frontend components via top-layer microstrip coupling gap feed. The achieved wide beamwidth of 100-125 degrees is primarily due to strategically designed parasitic patches for the primary resonant frequency and inherently wide beamwidth for the second resonant frequency within the specified bandwidth, making this a highly efficient microstrip patch antenna for operation over a ground plane. The input impedance and radiation pattern observed through measured data closely agree with the simulated results.

Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models.

Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics, often with notable results, but also with significant challenges, particularly instability and low signal quality. To overcome these issues, our method employs a two-cavity network to measure the relative phase in entangled states. By utilizing cavity enhancements and quantum jump detection, we can achieve remarkable precision without accompanying instability. This approach offers significant advantages and has the potential to be applied in a range of experiments.

The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions from 2006 to 2011. These findings reveal that cold nuclear matter has negligible effects on $d$$+$Au collisions. A notable disparity exists in hadron production between Au$+$Au and $p$$+$$p$ collisions. Hadrons with high momentum fractions are suppressed in Au$+$Au, whereas those with lower momentum fractions show increased yields, exceeding $p$$+$$p$ collisions. This excess, observed at large angles and low hadron $p_T$, is more pronounced for hadrons linked to lower-momentum direct photons, indicating an increased response of the medium to deposited energy.

In this hybrid digital-analog approach to quantum computing, any quantum algorithm can be implemented without traditional two-qubit gates by utilizing an inherent, always-active connection between qubits. Building on this principle, our research explores how digital-analog simulation can be used to study fermionic systems, specifically the Fermi-Hubbard model, using a fermionic SWAP network and a method to correct distortions. Focusing on the effects of qubit connectivity and the distribution of interaction coefficients, as well as the precision of entanglement-inducing operations, our results indicate that an optimal qubit connectivity arrangement for simulating fermionic systems of any dimensionality is a chain for systems without spin and a ladder for those with spin. This relatively straightforward connectivity arrangement makes the digital-analog method particularly appealing for fermionic quantum simulations.

A common issue in machine learning lies in striking a balance between optimizing performance and robustly handling out-of-distribution (OoD) scenarios. Certain methods rely on complex penalty terms that can be difficult to optimize, as they either over- or under-penalize the model's predictions. 

We introduce an approach that begins with networks initialized using a comprehensive feature set, allowing even basic models to achieve improved performance. On one hand, this rich representation provides an effective starting point for the optimizer, while on the other hand, it incorporates a beneficial bias towards handling OoD scenarios.

This robust feature set is generated using the Rich Feature Construction (RFC) algorithm, also known as Bonsai, which comprises a sequence of iterative training episodes. The algorithm is comprised of discovery episodes where a multi-objective optimization criterion is crafted alongside corresponding datasets, to prevent the model from leveraging features developed in previous iterations. Synthesis episodes then utilize knowledge distillation to require the model to represent all features previously discovered. 

Using the Bonsai representation to initialize the networks leads to six out-of-distribution methods consistently achieving superior performance on ColoredMNIST, surpassing comparable results on Wilds Camelyon17, while also substantially reducing result variability and streamlining hyperparameter tuning and model selection processes.

Achieving the formation of intricate structures and rapid concentration of light within or through disordered mediums is an arduous endeavor due to variations in refractive index, unpredictable light scattering, and speckle noise generation. To address these challenges, we've developed a novel weighted-mutation-assisted genetic algorithm (WMA-GA) with an R-squared-based fitness function that enhances image clarity, precision, and rapid convergence in forming complex structures within scattering media. As a companion technology to our binary WMA-GA system, we've designed a swift, economical, and reliable iterative wavefront manipulation system that utilizes an affordable ferroelectric liquid crystal (FLC)-based binary-phase spatial light modulator (SLM). This wavefront manipulation system enables the creation of numerous complex 3D heterostructures with an optimized single phase mask. We've verified the efficacy of our proposed approach with 120, 220, 450, and 600 grit ground glass diffusers, as well as with 323, 588, and 852 μm thick fresh chicken tissues including fluorescent properties. We've demonstrated the robustness of our proposed integrated system in controlling photon flow into and out of a localized fluorescent dye embedded in tissue. Detailed results reveal that our algorithm-driven integrated system achieves fast convergence and high image clarity with advanced resolution capabilities.

We appreciate the discussion opportunity facilitated by editors and valuable input from discussants. Our work is influenced by the inspiring research of Kallus (2020), which enhances policy learning efficiency via retargeting. Building upon Dukes and Vansteelandt (2020), we distinguish our research from Kallus (2020) in Section 1 by highlighting their distinct assumptions, variations, and research objectives. In Section 2, guided by Li et al. (2020) and Liang and Zhao (2020), we analyze the efficient policy evaluation problem using data from multiple periods, demonstrating our method's stronger assumptions and comparable results with Kallus (2020). In Section 3, driven by Li et al. (2020) and Liang and Zhao (2020) again, we explore efficient policy evaluation using data from multiple sources, which generalizes the prior result by Kallus (2020). In Section 4, we emphasize the scope of our research and outline potential future directions.

Monolithic CMOS sensors featuring small collection electrodes are advantageous due to high signal quality and low power consumption. However, these sensors have limited functionality due to the use of thin high-resistivity epitaxial layers during fabrication. In this study, researchers investigate the active sensor depth using the CLICTD technology, a small collection-electrode monolithic demonstrator. Particle beams are utilized to analyze the charge collection properties and device performance across different thicknesses under various beam angles. In CMOS sensors utilizing a high-resistivity Czochralski substrate, a notable enhancement is observed, with the sensitive volume increasing two-fold, subsequently yielding significant gains in detection efficiency and spatial/temporal resolution.

Advanced telescopes strive to spot planets at closer distances, lower masses, or older ages than ever before, with the ultimate goal of directly identifying habitable-zone planets with masses similar to those of Earth. Despite recent technological improvements, a significant barrier remains, with the ability of current high-tech ground-based telescopes limited by image speckles that obstruct our view. This challenge has made it difficult to effectively eliminate the distortions introduced by the atmosphere and the telescope's instruments themselves. To overcome this issue, researchers have proposed a new system known as the Fast Atmospheric Self-coherent camera (FAST), a wavefront sensing and control algorithm that enables the system to operate at the speed of milliseconds even when it detects extremely faint signals. We have successfully tested FAST in the laboratory, showcasing its capability to effectively eliminate the distortions introduced by the atmosphere at the speed of milliseconds.

This study presents a novel exogenous model to tackle the challenge of negative interest rates, maintaining the mathematical ease of the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model, and accurately replicating the observed yield curve. It combines the difference between two separate Cox-Ingersoll-Ross processes, incorporating the deterministic-shift adjustment. For quick alignment with the current swaption prices, the Gram-Charlier expansion is employed to calculate swaption prices within the proposed framework. Multiple numerical evaluations, conducted using Monte-Carlo simulations, demonstrate the effectiveness of this model, as well as the Gram-Charlier expansion, in pricing swaptions, particularly when the underlying interest rate process is subject to diverse regimes.

Research into the characteristics of neutrino oscillations using active neutrinos may also lead to discoveries about sterile neutrinos, specifically in their associated parameters. We investigate the potential of DUNE, a forthcoming experiment, in searching for sterile neutrinos with masses in the GeV range. Our findings rely on the design of DUNE's Near Detector, so we calculated the anticipated sterile neutrino decays within the detector's volume. According to our projections, DUNE may establish a limit comparable to past predictions made for LBNE. We visualize our results for each neutrino type – electron, muon, and tau – indicating that DUNE has a promising capacity to explore previously unexplored areas of sterile neutrino parameter space before the SHiP experiment joins similar research initiatives.

Meta-analyses that include multiple trials based on shared study participants often report correlated effect sizes.  In such scenarios, employing cluster-correlated meta-analysis or pseudo-cluster correlation corrections can provide accurate predictions of variance.  However, these methods might not always be applicable due to a lack of information about the sizes of clinical trials or the costs of obtaining this data.  In this research, we develop three new cluster robust estimators: the first relies on an unstructured correlation matrix, while the second assumes a specific pattern of correlation, both of these estimators require knowledge of trial sizes.  Alternatively, we suggest an estimator that doesn't require this information, which is based on the maximum likelihood estimate of cluster variance.  All of these estimators offer benefits when assessing the impact of a particular study.  We compared the performance of these estimators in realistic scenarios, using a realistic simulation study.  We further extended this research by integrating the new estimators into a variety of methods for meta-regression and conducting a comprehensive analysis of various combinations of data types and estimators, in the context of a real-world example involving the effects of cannabis on schizophrenia.

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy.

Investigating the source of radiation energy in the Unruh/Hawking process has shed new light on the particle number definition, particularly as it relates to conservation laws. Research has found that particle radiation is not a product of gravitational force-driven pair creation, but rather an outcome stemming from disparities in the laws governing particle number definition. In the far distant future, the source of emitted energy corresponds to zero-point fluctuations characterized by exponentially large wave numbers, prompting a reassessment of the black hole evaporation paradigm.

The effect of transverse momentum broadening on parton propagation through a large nucleus is investigated using various models in the color dipole framework. These models generate different values of a key coefficient that influence broadening calculations. Results obtained via numerical analysis are then compared with LHCb and ALICE experimental findings for nuclear broadening in the context of J/Psi particles. Notably, models that align with small-x data are shown to yield transverse momentum variations consistent with measured values, especially in cases where rapidity is in the forward direction. Additionally, model consistency with ALICE measurements is found across various centrality levels.

This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$.

The video explores the dynamics of a liquid jet that enters a channel filled with the same fluid. As the jet interacts with the surrounding stream, it becomes encircled by a sheath of entrained air. This sheath plays a significant role in the dynamic behavior of the jet and its penetration into the stream. Additionally, we examine the instability effects that develop on the liquid jet and the consequences of these effects on its behavior in the context of fluid dynamics.

High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault tolerance to prevent data loss and ensure system reliability. Recent advances in non-volatile memory technology have made it feasible to achieve this, as data in such memory is preserved even during crashes. Nevertheless, the volatility of system caches still poses a challenge, as data in these caches may be lost in the event of a crash, necessitating an explicit flush into the main memory to guarantee data integrity. In this study, a new algorithm-based approach is proposed to guarantee data consistency and correctness for high-performance computing applications in systems using non-volatile memory. This method introduces only a minor runtime overhead, allowing developers to leverage the properties of algorithms to verify data integrity after system crashes. Our proposed approach demonstrates significant advantages over traditional checkpointing methods in terms of runtime efficiency while maintaining the ability to correct errors with minimal reprocessing costs. Our comprehensive evaluations, carried out across multiple test scenarios and algorithms such as an iterative solver and dense matrix multiplication, have consistently yielded a remarkably low overhead, amounting to just 1-3% in many cases, thereby making this approach an attractive solution for ensuring fault-tolerant HPC applications.

Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content.

We conducted an exhaustive examination comparing the statistical properties of non-hierarchical three-body systems with corresponding theoretical models. By running and analyzing one million simulations for diverse initial conditions, both with and without equal masses in three-body systems, we were able to achieve precise statistical accuracy. Four distinct measures were used to characterize the distribution of ergodic disintegrations: the probability of escape for individual bodies, the exponent representing narrow escapes, the predicted absorption as a function of binary energy and angular momentum, and the distribution of lifetimes. Our results showed that escape probabilities matched theoretical predictions with high precision, marking a significant improvement over previous statistical theories. Furthermore, the measured values of the exponent near the margin of escape for each body aligned well with the flux-based statistical model's prediction. Both theoretical models, when applied to the distribution of absorptions, explained nearly 90% of the variance in three-body system properties. Lastly, the measured lifetime distribution, when filtered to exclude close approaches, demonstrated a 0.98 correlation with the predicted function using two distinct variables.

Measurements of the nuclear modification factors of J/$\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) mesons were made in collisions of lead ions at the Large Hadron Collider in 2015. The study was based on data from both lead-lead and proton-proton collisions, involving a total of 5.02 TeV per nucleon pair. The findings show that suppression of both prompt and non-prompt mesons increases with the level of collision centrality, at an extent comparable to that found in 2.76 TeV collisions. The study also reveals a significant suppression of J/$\psi$ production in ultra-central collisions, amounting to 45 percent or more. The findings are consistent with the idea that the formation of charmonium states at the LHC involves both prompt creation by quark collisions and a temperature-driven hadronization of heavier states such as charmonium and D mesons.

We propose an arrangement of predicates in continuous logic such that the
logical framework's meaning can be structured within a hyperdoctrine framework.
This hyperdoctrine can be incorporated into a hyperdoctrine representing subobjects within a suitable category of topological structures. 
To achieve this incorporation, we first simplify the hyperdoctrine framework for continuous logic and establish an equivalence between its category of equivalence relations and that of complete metric spaces under uniform mappings.

When designing a software system, a modification in one component may
unintentionally impact other parts, hindering overall system performance. This is
addressed by conducting regression testing, which re-evaluates system sections
aimed at preventing adverse effects. However, pinpointing these affected areas
proves challenging, making it essential to identify system changes through a
different approach. We apply singular value decomposition to group software
modifications by their functional roles, allowing for more efficient detection
of areas requiring retesting during subsequent updates. By leveraging parallel
calculations on shared memory systems, we enhance testing speed, and therefore,
effective system testing velocity.

A new technique is proposed to forecast suicidal ideation based on the integration of Electronic Health Records and Ecological Momentary Assessment data utilizing advanced deep sequential models. These datasets consist of asynchronous, variable-length, randomly sampled sequences which are modelled separately using Recurrent Neural Networks and combined through the alignment of hidden states, along with attention and pre-training schemes to handle differing sequence lengths. Experimental outcomes using 1023 patients' data demonstrate that the incorporation of Ecological Momentary Assessment records significantly increases the recall of the model in predicting suicidal ideation, from 48.1% using Electronic Health Record data alone to 67.8%. Furthermore, the proposed method offers enhanced interpretability through dimensionality reduction in the latent space and medical feature analysis.

Our research reports a significant $\sim 5\sigma$ discovery of polarized X-ray emission within a range of 3-6 keV originating from Cassiopeia A with the IXPE. Our findings reveal a combined polarization level of $1.8 \pm 0.3$%, yielding a significance level of $5.3\sigma$. The polarization angle and magnitude found to be steady across different energy ranges, suggesting that they are consistent. Analysis of the polarization data suggests that it originates from a mixture of thermal and non-thermal components with contributions from the supernova's ejecta and forward-shocked material. The detection of a weak polarization signal within the 3-6 keV range suggests that a small fraction of radioactive $^{56}$Ni has been injected into the ejecta with an estimated lower limit of around 0.3 mx. The polarization angle and magnitude found to be stable at different energy ranges imply a unified origin for the X-rays within the supernova remnant. The certain polarization detection within the 3-6 keV range implies that a small fraction of radioactive $^{56}$Ni has been injected into the ejecta with an estimated lower limit of around 0.3 mx.

Consider a set $\{a_1, \ldots, a_n\}$ of distinct positive integers where $a_1 < \ldots < a_n$, with the requirement that only subset sums up to a size of at most $\lambda n$ be unique. Erdos originally proposed a conjecture suggesting that $a_n > c \cdot 2^n$, with the current record at $a_n > c \cdot 2^n/\sqrt{n}$. This article presents modified constraints where we investigate lower and upper bounds for the minimum possible value of $a_n$.

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are intriguingly ambiguous and may influence neutron star dynamics as detected via gravitational waves.  As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed. It's hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, possibly exhibiting a distinctive relationship with density. Our work delves into the fundamental properties of dense matter sound velocity and the adiabatic index within neutron stars, quark stars, and hybrid stars.  By simulating the hadron-quark phase transition with different interface tension, we found the sound velocity's expected behavior could also arise from the quark phase's nonperturbative properties, specifically from the instanton potential, thus eliminating the need for density where quark deconfinement occurs. Additionally, our research reveals that compact stars comprising only nonrelativistic matter can't meet the causality constraint, implying that dense matter's underlying physical nature is relativistic. This research provides new specifications for compact star density, sound velocity, and adiabatic index, offering fresh insights into the dense matter that governs compact stars.

We investigate a variety of non-classical states made up of superposed, both squeezed and displaced number states, examining their phase space structure in relation to Heisenberg limited sensitivity in parameter estimation. Certain combinations of squeezing and displacement are identified that maintain over 99% state fidelity compared to a highly sensitive reference state, known as a compass state, which also exhibits equivalent variance in small shifts measurements. Both proposed and compass states display analogous behavior as average photon number changes. Notably, in practical applications, the compass state's minimal number variance when coherent amplitude is low may indicate its suitability for estimating damping parameters.

During gas-liquid interfaces that are subject to irregular movement such as splashing and atomization, the resulting fluid structures can be intricate and embedded in their surroundings. In this work, we employ a technique called skeletonization to extract the fundamental information needed to represent their geometry. By applying a modified version of a previous approach that efficiently captures the dynamics of multi-component flows with distinct interfaces, we successfully simplify the representation of a periodic liquid jet. This involves propagating a gradient through the structure and simultaneously adjusting its interfaces, ultimately leading to their convergence into the essential framework of the jet's morphology. This framework, which represents the fundamental structure of the jet, is coupled with a quantitative assessment of the interfaces' displacement or volume modification throughout the process, thereby facilitating the reconstruction of the original jet configuration. Furthermore, we evaluate several metrics to classify and differentiate the resulting frameworks. These measures encompass conventional parameters such as branch length distribution following their division into constituent parts, as well as a more advanced representation of the structure known as Topology Morphology Descriptor (TMD), which generates an equivalent representation of the structures by encoding the spatial topology into a concise format.

Researchers discovered that certain influenza viruses exhibit active movement on surfaces with carbohydrate layers by rolling along them, as shown in recent studies. This phenomenon was previously proposed to be an example of viral surface metabolism, where the collection of spike proteins interacts with the carbohydrates, generating mechanical movement through a self-organizing process. This research aims to investigate in greater detail the physical aspects underlying this rolling motion, developing a theory that explains the motor's behavior, as well as validating the results using simulations to analyze the impact of various factors. The outcomes of this study strongly indicate that viral movement on surfaces can be accurately predicted using a simplified model, confirming the hypothesis that surface metabolism is the primary driver of this behavior.

We examined over 8,000 massive, edge-on disk galaxies from the SDSS dataset, focusing on two types: S and U galaxies. Our analysis revealed that U galaxies have distinct characteristics, including bluer optical colors and higher star formation rates, compared to S galaxies. U galaxies, particularly those with more extreme warping, exhibited higher star formation rates. Contrary to expectations, U galaxies in groups and clusters do not show a correlation with the tidal force exerted by their nearest neighbor. However, U galaxies are more common in groups and clusters and share similarities with 'jellyfish' galaxies formed through ram-pressure stripping (RPS). This led us to suggest that RPS could be a potential mechanism explaining the presence of U galaxies in groups and clusters.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional.

Compounds composed of potassium ($A=$ K, Rb, Cs) combined with boron in a 2:1 ratio, exhibit unique cubic structures called the Laves phase with a specific Fd$\bar{3}$m symmetry. The arrangement of atoms within these crystals permits the existence of chirally behaving phonons, which correspond to atoms circling their equilibrium positions. Given that the total number of phonon polarization directions is determined by dimensions and not the type, all phonon modes can exhibit this circular motion. The proposed theory suggests that the total number of unique phonon modes is further increased by the availability of multiple available crystallographic sites. This concept has significant potential in developing technologies utilizing phonons, as they allow for the creation of circular light polarization without employing magnetic materials and offer a means to achieve full control over the optical response through the manipulation of phonon beams at the nanoscale.

In insulators, Born effective charges relate to how the positioning of individual atomic sublattices generates electric polarization, a concept seemingly unrelated to metals and doped semiconductors. However, our findings reveal that, when the conventional approximation is surpassed, nonadiabatic Born effective charges become well defined in metals within a specific frequency range. We also observe that, unlike in insulators, the summation of nonadiabatic Born effective charges from sublattices in metals does not equal zero but rather correlates directly with the Drude weight. These conclusions were verified through calculations using density functional perturbation theory, as applied to aluminum, and to two doped compounds, electron-doped tin disulfide and strontium titanate.

We are reassessing the significance of thermal fluctuations in incompressible fluid turbulence and determining their relevance on a particular scale. As earlier research by Betchov predicted decades ago, this scale is equivalent to the Kolmogorov length, although it's still many orders of magnitude greater than the average free path. This finding suggests that the non-random, or deterministic, form of the Navier-Stokes equation is insufficient for modeling the turbulence dissipation range within molecular fluids. Instead, the fluctuating hydrodynamics equation by Landau and Lifschitz provides a more accurate description within this range. Specifically, our analysis implies that the exponentially decaying energy spectrum and the extreme intermittency in the far-dissipation range of turbulence predicted by deterministic Navier-Stokes equations will generally be replaced by Gaussian thermal equipartition at scales below the Kolmogorov length. High-Reynolds-number simulations based on the stochastic shell model corroborate our theoretical predictions, and demonstrate that the extreme intermittency in the inertial range can extend deeply into the dissipation range, leading to large variations in the thermal equipartition threshold. Our study addresses a long-standing, open issue in turbulence and high-Reynolds-number fluid dynamics.

Three-dimensional topological insulators can be identified by a magnetoelectric coefficient with a quantized value, but it lacks observable manifestations when time-reversal symmetry prevails due to opposing influences of internal and external states cancelling out. The distinctive response characteristic of a topological insulator manifests as a nonlinear magnetoelectric effect, whose field-theoretical properties and computational models are explored. This contrasts with another phenomenon where a magnetoelectric interaction traps a charge equal to $\pm e/2$ upon exposure to a magnetic monopole, commonly referred to as the Witten effect. The time-reversal symmetry being explicitly violated, as in the case of a Zeeman field influencing the surface electrons, can allow a description of a topological insulator's electromagnetic response via the surface electrons undergoing a half-integer quantum Hall effect.

In systems featuring delayed nonlinearity, we observe chaotic diffusion as a typical trait, where it is found that modulating the time delay periodically leads to a significant enhancement of the diffusion coefficient by several orders of magnitude, especially when the modulation's map exhibits mode locking, characteristic of laminar chaos. For the first time, we establish a link between Arnold tongue patterns in parameter space and the diffusive behavior of delay systems. Contrary to expectation, this increase in diffusion is accompanied by a considerable decrease in the system's effective dimensionality.

We provide rigorous definitions for sound and sufficient denotational and operational interpretations of the stochastic lambda calculus. By adapting established techniques to reason about high-level probabilistic code, this study achieves a breakthrough in linking operational and denotational views with a proven adequacy theorem, thereby closing a key outstanding issue identified in earlier work (Bacci et al., 2018).

Discussions among developers encompass a variety of interactions, including in-person conversations and online comments, which are beneficial to label as relevant to software design for documentation and improvement purposes. This is made possible through a process known as design mining, which applies machine learning to categorize discussions as pertaining to design. This paper showcases a simple model for design mining, revealing that current methods suffer from inconsistent conclusions on various discussion types and projects. We then introduce and demonstrate two effective techniques - data enrichment and project adaptation - that enhance design mining's reliability and adaptability across different datasets, achieving a satisfactory classification rate of 0.88 within a dataset and 0.80 across different datasets.

A proposed model explains the existence of gravity, dark energy, and dark matter.
Dark energy and dark matter stem from a false vacuum state's random energy fluctuations, characterized by large-scale negative and short-scale positive pressures, respectively, representing incoherent and coherent aspects of a superfluid/supersolid state.
Gravity emerges from topological defects within the post-inflation virtual "condensate" component.
Consequently, it is anticipated that exotic particles that could explain dark matter will not be detected at the LHC.
Moreover, a de Sitter point corresponds to a superfluid/supersolid's liquid/solid phase transition boundary, while black holes represent frozen topological defects.
Following the suggestion that our universe's initial state must be specified by its initial entropy rather than the wave function, it is claimed that gravity, dark energy, and dark matter derive organically from the post-inflation virtual "condensate" – a de Sitter-dominated superfluid/supersolid state.
Ultimately, it is contended that the fundamental physical laws comprise the supersymmetric post-inflation holographic Higgs-Goldstone model.

Proximal methods can efficiently uncover the underlying pattern in nonsmooth optimization problems, and, in many cases, identifying this structure is a free byproduct, also enhancing the convergence rate once aligned with that of the problem's optimal solution. Nonetheless, pinpointing the exact structure is not possible without adaptation. By assuming a proximal gradient method is able to recognize the differentiability manifolds in a nonsmooth objective, we show that incorporating Riemannian Newton-like techniques alongside the proximal gradient steps results in a significantly improved convergence rate for specific nondegenerated nonsmooth nonconvex optimization problems. Moreover, our algorithm is accompanied by a numerical study that includes optimizations regulated by $\ell_1$-norm and trace-norm.

We are introducing a new concept called weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals within a commutative ring with identity, which serves as an extension to the existing notion of weakly prime ideals. A prime ideal $I$ in a ring $R$ is said to be weakly $1$-absorbing if for every three non-unit elements $a,b,$ and $c$ in $R$ where their product is non-zero and within $I$, it follows that either the product of $a$ and $b$ is in $I$, or $c$ is in $I$. Our research presents numerous results regarding the characteristics and examples of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals. It has been proven that if $I$ is a weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideal in a ring $R$ where the product of three non-zero ideals is completely contained in $I$, it then holds that either the product of the first two ideals is completely contained in $I$, or the third ideal is completely contained in $I$. Additionally, it is demonstrated that if $I$ is not a $1$-absorbing prime ideal in a ring $R$ but a weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideal, then $I^3 = 0$. Furthermore, the characteristics of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals within principal ideal domains and Dedekind domains have been determined

We present new findings for two semileptonic decay processes, $B^0$ decaying into $\rho^-$ and a lepton-neutrino pair, and $B^+$ decaying into $\rho^0$ with the same pair, utilizing data from Belle II's sample equivalent to 189.9/fb, collected using the SuperKEKB $e^-e^+$ collider. To identify these decays, the research involved reconstructing the full recoil B-meson within hadronic end products, after which the researchers computed total branching ratios by performing statistical fits on missing mass square and dipion mass in the candidate signal, determining the former to be $4.12 \pm 0.64 (stat.) \pm 1.16 (syst.) \times 10^{-4}$ and the latter as $1.77 \pm 0.23 (stat.) \pm 0.36 (syst.) \times 10^{-4}$. These findings are primarily subject to systematic error due to nonresonant influences on B-meson decay patterns.

Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional method of spectroscopy, enabling on-device spectral cross-correlation using a template spectrum. This was achieved by designing photonic devices with intricately modulated transmission spectra, thus performing cross-correlation without the need for dispersion. Consequently, our device simplifies the apparatus while reducing its overall cost, as demonstrated by our successful prototype examples.

We describe a research challenge, outline our design framework, and present a selection of our experimental results, which showcase various photonic devices based on different materials, including planar photonic waves, resonant cavities, and rare-earth doped photonic systems. These examples showcase our successful application of photonic technology to spectral analysis, enabling rapid and efficient assessments of spectral structures.

Through our research, we have developed a comprehensive database of spectral templates and associated photonic devices, which can be accessed via an online tool. This resource will facilitate the development of innovative photonic applications, as it enables researchers to quickly identify and implement spectroscopic techniques that leverage photonic technology.

Ultimately, our research seeks to translate the control offered by photonic technology over light propagation within these devices into a comparable control over complex data sets, thereby enabling a more intuitive understanding of data and a more efficient analysis.

In the last few years, various machine learning models have emerged with the aim of tackling polypharmacy side effects, predicting medication interactions, and optimizing combination therapies. This paper takes a comprehensive approach, offering a theoretical framework that can address these challenges through relational machine learning models. It provides key concepts, assesses existing model architectures, discusses relevant evaluation metrics, datasets, and testing protocols. Furthermore, it highlights significant potential applications and suggests vital research paths for the future in this field.

Several local authorities face challenges in deploying advanced automated
evaluation of road damage due to a lack of necessary technology, expertise, and
financial resources for sophisticated equipment. While countries like Japan have
introduced more cost-effective and accessible smartphone-based solutions for
automated road condition monitoring, many other countries continue to search for
efficient alternatives. To address these issues, this study contributes in
several key ways. Firstly, it examines the suitability of Japan's approach for
global implementation. Secondly, a substantial, multi-national smartphone-based
dataset consisting of 26,620 images is developed. Thirdly, a set of adaptable
models capable of detecting and classifying road damage in multiple countries is
proposed. Lastly, recommendations are provided for other countries seeking to
adopt successful strategies from their peers. The created dataset is available at
https://github.com/sekilab/RoadDamageDetector/.

Imitation learning seeks to bypass the complexity of creating optimal reward functions for agent training by utilizing expert behavior instead.  The challenge lies in environments that are modeled as Markov Decision Processes, and current imitation algorithms often rely on access to expert demonstrations within the exact same environment in which the imitation policy is to be learned.  However, when discrepancies arise between the source and target domains, imitation tasks become increasingly difficult.  To tackle this issue, we present a new framework that establishes connections between states across different domains, using the expert's behavior to align these states through a optimization process.  This approach, called Cross-Domain Imitation from Observations (CDIO), facilitates learning the imitation policy without the need for expert interactions within the target domain.  CDIO is based on two main components: aligning states using expert behavior and developing a target-specific imitation policy.  To solve the domain shift problem, CDIO employs a state alignment algorithm based on mutual information maximization, where the source and target domains exchange information to establish correspondences between states.  Once the states are aligned, CDIO creates a virtual target state space and generates target-specific trajectories by aggregating the aligned states and sampling actions from the target domain's past experiences.  This approach demonstrates effective imitation capabilities in a range of tasks, including navigation and pushing objects in 2D and 3D domains.

A major uncertainty in determining the initial mass function of the first (Population III) stars lies in predicting the secondary mass distribution resulting from the fragmentation of protostellar disks. Studies of accretion and disk fragmentation have shown that a small number of secondary fragments could form, with masses comparable to those of Population III stars. However, determining the exact mass distribution of these fragments remains uncertain. We investigate the effect of amplification of the magnetic field in the disk, due to dynamo action, on the fragmentation of the protostellar disk. We conduct a series of simulations, using the AMR code Starry Sky, for different magnetic field amplification levels and those resulting from the BOK cycle. The outcome of these simulations demonstrate that a significantly strong magnetic field, above a certain threshold, prevents the fragmentation of the protostellar disk. We observe no mass distribution of secondary fragments in our study, as all massive eruptions are eliminated by the strong magnetic field. We predict that a zero to extremely low initial mass function for Population III stars could result from this mechanism alone.

Association rule analysis is a widely used technique in Data Mining. This method involves partial implications between binary variables and has been applied in numerous real-world scenarios. We explore the concept of redundancy in association rules from a logical perspective. By defining rule redundancy, we identify key deduction schemes and develop a method to identify the smallest possible bases for these schemes.

Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1992 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who received court-ordered mental health treatment against those who did not require such treatment.  It is essential to note that this analysis does not include offenders who were incarcerated, had their probation revoked, or died.  The study discovered several key findings.  Firstly, receiving court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation increased the chances of an offender being convicted of another crime by 4 percentage points and reduced the chances of the offender completing their probation by 4 to 5 percentage points compared to those who did not require such treatment.  Furthermore, the effects of court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation varied based on several key variables including but not limited to the offender's prior convictions, physical health, relationship status, and the level of supervision as part of their probation.  An initial analysis of data suggested that the likelihood of conviction within a two-year period was at its highest for those offenders who were given court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation who had no prior convictions (11.7 percentage points higher) whereas the likelihood of conviction within a two-year period was at its lowest for those offenders who were given court-ordered

The authors of the paper delve into generalized Apostol-Bernoulli polynomials with parameters, derive their generating functions, examine key properties and relationships, and establish connections to other notable polynomials.

Radio maps are being explored as a promising approach to equip advanced wireless networks with situational awareness. They will likely serve a pivotal function in enabling UAV communications by allowing the assessment of signal strength and interference levels at unknown locations. Different from conventional radio map estimation techniques, which depend on uncontrolled sensor measurements, a new method proposes that a UAV collect data at designated locations along a carefully planned route to quickly obtain a reliable map. This route is optimized using a measure that identifies the most informative locations to collect data from. A novel real-time Bayesian algorithm has been created to constantly update the map estimate and the associated uncertainty metric with every new data point, allowing the process to take place in real-time.

This paper outlines a novel approach, GLA, for identifying unusual patterns in discrete time series by leveraging Hidden Markov Models and clustering techniques. At its core lies the comparison of sequential data segments. The process involves first grouping similar sequences and then scanning for sets with significantly disparate distributions of transitions. Typically, a statistical anomaly detection method would proceed from here to filter out false positives. Notably, the proposed GLA method excels at accurately capturing these false positives, thus reducing its reliance on subsequent processing. The algorithm's effectiveness is further demonstrated through its application to real-world data.

This research delves into a multi-aspect approach to person verification incorporating auditory, visual, and thermal modalities. Given the efficacy of auditory and visual modality combination, this investigation extends to exploring the effect of incorporating thermal images on verification robustness. Specifically, state-of-the-art deep learning architectures were applied to establish unimodal, bimodal, and trimodal verification systems which were compared under optimal and impaired conditions. Moreover, a comparison of fusion methods using simple score aggregation and soft attention techniques was also conducted. Experimental results obtained on the SpeakingFaces dataset showed that a multi-aspect verification system outperforms unimodal and bimodal approaches by significant margins, both in noise-free and noise-present scenarios. To promote research in the area and guarantee replicability of this research, our source code, pre-trained models, and dataset preprocessed for analysis were made freely accessible on our GitHub repository.

Generating new training data through augmentation is achieved by appending existing examples to create new instances. We've found this approach to be both simple and cost-effective in boosting the performance of pre-optimized Transformer and Conformer models. Specifically, enhancements of up to 2.83 WER and 6.87 WER are seen in the LibriSpeech-960h test sets, and even higher when models were combined with fusion. Moreover, improvements of as much as 0.9 WER are recorded on the CoVoST-2 for several non-English languages following this training methodology. Notably, results indicate the extent of gain heavily depends on the quality of initial data. We've also demonstrated the effectiveness of this training method on other datasets, such as Voxforge and CoVoST-2 for speech translation. Furthermore, our research shows data augmentation to be a viable supplement to other techniques, like specAugment, which can be considered a form of data augmentation. Ultimately, data augmentation presents a versatile tool for enhancing model performance with a high degree of cost-efficiency.

Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by $f(y|\theta)$ where the parameter $\theta$ needs to be estimated. When data follows a mixture model of these distributions with unknown mixing probabilities, traditional maximum likelihood estimation can't be applied directly.
