This paper explores whether estimating the mixture probabilities and the distribution parameters separately is viable and develops conditions to ensure this is possible. Our results are applied to various distribution families, including the binary, binomial, negative binomial, Poisson, normal and Cauchy distributions. Our findings are further tested using simulated data. Additionally, we demonstrate the feasibility of using our estimated parameters to estimate the mean of a mixture distribution. Our analysis addresses both population and sampling scenarios.

Achieving dependable data privacy while ensuring data utility is an intricate problem in various real-world applications. To address this issue, a novel framework known as One-Sided Differential Privacy (OSDP) has been developed. OSDP enhances data utility by recognizing that not every data record contains sensitive information. However, the previous approaches in this field made the assumption that data records were statistically independent from one another. Inspired by occupancy data analysis in building management systems, the current research builds upon the one-sided differential privacy framework by accounting for inter-record dependencies. Furthermore, the paper quantifies total privacy breaches when the adversary possesses record interdependence information, as well as demonstrates the creation of an optimization problem for an efficient trade-off between utility and privacy.

In protoplanetary disks, it is not unusual to come across gas and dust emission substructures.
These substructures may have connections to the formation of planets themselves.
Our investigation into the AS 209 gas substructures employed thermochemical modeling using RAC2D and precise observations from the Molecules with ALMA at Planet-forming Scales project.
Our observations of C$^{18}$O showed that the disk's gas surface density may be lower than previously estimated, especially in areas close to the disk's midplane and outer regions.
Our models aimed to explain various observed species, taking into account the physical and chemical evolution of the disk over time.
It is observed that the disk's inner regions display lower CO surface densities compared to its outer areas.
This CO surface density decrease could be the result of gas being depleted due to accretion or photo-dissociation from the conserving beam.
Our models, however, showed that a complete destruction of the CO molecule is not feasible.
Our models further revealed that the inner regions' CO depletion could be the result of CO being broken down into atomic carbon under the influence of nearby hot gas streams or a large planet.
This CO surface density decrease could also be the result of gas being processed by a growing protoplanet leading to CO dissociation.

The analysis of time-stamped data is a fundamental aspect of scientific and industrial research, where the vast amount of generated data poses significant processing challenges due to increased resolution, input channels, and event acquisition rates. To overcome these obstacles, we've created the Extensible Time-tag Analyzer (ETA), an advanced, yet intuitive software solution that streamlines time-stamped data analysis and visualization. Leveraging an integrated approach of flowcharts and modular code snippets, our tool empowers users to perform intricate data correlation and analysis, while maintaining high computational performance and efficiency.

We prove the existence of'mild solutions' for a mean field game involving first-order controls with a constraint requiring state and control trajectories remain within a closed, bounded Euclidean space area. This outcome builds upon Cannarsa and Capuani's research, adapting it to apply to mean field games of controls with velocities as controls. The existence of an equilibrium in this context is challenged by requiring the necessary regularity of controls, a requirement we overcome by imposing a small Lipschitz constraint on the dependence of the Lagrangian function on the joint measure of states and controls, and showing that under these constraints regular paths can be closely approximated.

Recent analyses of Gaia data have led to the discovery of new stellar structures, a newly classified type known as stellar "strings". We conducted an in-depth examination of these structures, focusing on their spatial patterns, movement, chemical composition, and whether their members originated from a shared location. By analyzing the distribution of these structures in 3D space, we discovered that they do not exhibit improved spatial alignment as expected in real, interconnected structures, contrary to earlier assumptions. Calculating the masses of these structures based on their radial velocity dispersion revealed that they are actually not gravitationally bound. Furthermore, we found that these structures' ages, when compared to their actual age spread, appear excessively large. It is also worth noting that these structures, while seemingly homogeneous, can exhibit identical characteristics if composed of randomly selected stars from separate clusters, indicating that these structures might be mere coincidences. These findings call for a cautious interpretation of these structures' significance in understanding the star formation history of the Milky Way galaxy.

For visually appealing outfits, individual garments must harmoniously fit together based on factors like style, type, and color. Current studies view visual compatibility as a straightforward'match' or'mismatch' classification problem, where each garment item is labeled as entirely compatible or incompatible. Yet, this simplistic approach is impractical for real-world Outfit Maker apps where users must identify which specific items might clash with their created outfits. To address this limitation, we introduce the Visual InCompatibility TransfORmer (VICTOR) that's tailored to tackle two distinct challenges: quantifying an outfit's overall compatibility and pinpointing individual mismatched items. Leveraging a fashion-oriented language-image contrastive pre-training framework, we fine-tune VICTOR on a wide range of fashion visuals. We expand the existing fashion research by introducing the individual mismatch detection task, evaluating VICTOR's performance on the Fashionista dataset, and providing detailed insights into its results. Furthermore, we demonstrate VICTOR's practical applications in creating "almost perfect" outfits by removing a few items from an existing outfit, thus besting existing methods.

The framework of quantum resource theory has significantly advanced quantum physics, enabling the unification of diverse methods to quantify specific quantum effects. It plays a pivotal role in optimizing their utility across various applications. The incorporation of radical quantum phenomena such as coherence, entanglement, and nonclassicality has enabled their application in real-world contexts. The theoretical framework of quantum resource theory categorizes quantum states into 'free' and'resource' sets. Operations associated with free states emerge naturally from the system's constraints, whereas resource theories aim to discover and harness the potential within the restricted set. Recent breakthroughs in the field of standard harmonic oscillator quantum states have sparked rapid growth and advancements in the generalized quantum optical framework. The incorporation of contemporary ideas such as nonlinearity, non-Hermitian theories, and $q$-deformed bosonic systems aims to achieve elevated objectives in the field of quantum information. This article reviews recent developments in the resource theories of generalized quantum optical states and their applications in the realm of quantum information.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis of the modified FedBuff algorithm considers factors like diverse data sets, varying batch sizes, and delay intervals.

This study introduces a functional calculus tailored to a countable set of operators generating contraction strongly continuous semigroups. We select polynomial tempered distributions as the symbol class for this calculus. We then establish a key differential property and elucidate its mapping in relation to the commutant of a polynomial shift semigroup. As a concrete demonstration of its utility, we examine the function of a countable set of second derivative operators.

Recent research suggests combining the Swampland program with dark energy's scarcity could predict the presence of an additional dimension with a characteristic scale of a micron. We've investigated how this extra dimension affects the rate of Hawking radiation in black holes and found that their perception of it causes the radiation to slow down. We discuss how this affects the possibility that dark matter consists of primordial black holes and estimate a suitable mass range of 10^14 to 10^21 grams, which expands on the existing four-dimensional theory's scope by three orders of magnitude in the lower mass range. Furthermore, the potential disappearance of black holes through the transfer of information to other parts of the Dark Dimension could extend the black hole lifetime by several orders of magnitude.

A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. Due to the slow timescales, both how the particles move back to a more stable configuration and the formation of cracks within the raft can be measured precisely. When we extend a raft made of particles by expanding its surface of support, we see that its breaking pattern changes constantly based on the rate at which we are stretching it. This effect is caused by the ongoing balance between two speed factors: the rate at which the particles reassemble, which is influenced by forces like viscosity and surface tension, and the rate at which neighboring particles move apart due to the stretching of the raft. This balance shift leads to a prediction that the breaking pattern will change suddenly at a specific point on the stretching scale, which we can reach by manipulating the stretching speed. This conclusion is supported by both theoretical modeling and experimental results showing that the breaking pattern transitions from a uniform to a periodic breakdown as we increase the stretching speed, corresponding to a shift towards higher viscosities. Additionally, we found that the distance between cracks in the raft follows a linear progression when we increase the stretching speed, which is also affected by the ratio of surface tension to viscosities. This behavior can be attributed to the existence of standing waves that form at the raft's surface as it is stretched, which govern the breaking pattern and provide a useful framework for analyzing this phenomenon.

The main challenge hindering the advancement of integrated gallium nitride electronics lies in its low hole mobility. In our investigation, we consider whether the mobility can be enhanced through epitaxial matching of GaN to certain II-IV nitride materials. We performed detailed computations utilizing the ab initio Boltzmann transport equation to calculate the hole mobility of GaN, revealing that aligning GaN under uniaxial compressive strain by matching it to ZnGeN$_2$ or MgSiN$_2$ inorganic materials flips the order of the heavy and light hole bands, resulting in a reduced hole mobility along one axis while increasing it on the perpendicular axis. Moreover, our data indicate that matching GaN to ZnGeN$_2$ yields a higher hole mobility compared to aligning it with MgSiN$_2$. We further observed that both cases exhibit higher hole mobility than that of GaN that is perfectly lattice-matched to silicon carbide. We ultimately demonstrated that matching GaN to ZnGeN$_2$ offers the potential to increase the hole mobility by a factor of 2.5 compared to its conventional value.

Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater.  By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods.  By deriving the posterior of the value function and utilizing its moments, we developed SPGP-SARSA: a new algorithm for offline policy evaluation.  Our results show that SPGP-SARSA outperforms the existing state-of-the-art in sparse methods and matches the accuracy of its precise equivalent while successfully being applied to underwater navigation.  Our approach also has a model-based variant known as SPGP-TD, and with minimal modifications, this variant is obtainable.  Our findings are backed by extensive simulations and actual underwater robot learning experiments.

We examine isothermic surfaces with a Hopf differential that decomposes into a real function and a specific quadratic differential with a singular point. However, this differential is nonzero and holomorphic throughout the rest of the surface except at this singular point. By focusing on a patch excluding the singular point, we find new isothermic surfaces applying the Darboux and Calapso transformations. Furthermore, we investigate how the transformed patches behave as they approach the singular point and check for continuity in that region.

We analyze the statistical approximation of the $L^2$-operator defined as $[Pf](x) = \mathbb{E}[f(Y) | X = x]$ given the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$ on a certain topological space under minimal assumptions. We modify its variant, which involves a data set $\{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$, by weighing the accuracy of this approximation using a data-dependent technique. This leads us to investigate a regularized version of the above operator, $\widehat{P}_n$, which possesses operator norm convergence and rate of convergence properties. These results are applicable to various nonparametric statistical settings, including imputation methods, inverse classification, conditional estimation, and target density estimation.

This paper builds upon recent studies by Kim-Kim on the $\lambda$-analogues of $r$-Stirling numbers of the first kind. We explore and define the $\lambda$-analogues of $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind and their associated properties. We derive recurrence relations, identities and present comparable results for $\lambda$-analogues of Whitney-type $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind. We also introduce $\lambda$-analogues of Dowling polynomials and provide a formula reminiscent of the Dobinski-like formula.

The consideration of temporal contexts within knowledge graph embeddings presents a chance for enhanced performance in resultant models, and consequently, in applications that rely on these embeddings. Despite this opportunity, previous research has given it little attention, and models developed to account for time frames often show only slight improvements over their static counterparts. Rather than adapting static models, many current studies have created new models designed specifically for temporal knowledge graphs. We propose an alternative approach, SpliMe, that takes advantage of the effectiveness of existing static models by modifying the input data. Our method is informed by the techniques of signal processing and past work in graph embeddings, and is presented as a simple, efficient solution that is unaffected by the size of the knowledge graph. Our experimental findings confirm that SpliMe delivers superior performance when compared to methods that incorporate time frames or rely on static models, and as such, it is a very competent temporal knowledge graph embedding method.

This note enhances and reinforces Bates' theorem which indicates that for row-finite graphs classified as strong shift equivalent, their associated graph C*-algebras are also Morita equivalent. This discovery opens up possibilities to investigate if the stronger notion of Morita equivalence effectively describes strong shift equivalence. This line of inquiry will likely hold significant value for ongoing research regarding infinite graphs and their associated C*-algebras. Moreover, this note specifically explores insplits and outsplits as key examples of strong shift equivalences, demonstrating that these equivalences lead to Morita equivalences that maintain consistency across various weighted gauge actions. Consequently, a question is raised about whether strong shift equivalence can be expressed as a product of insplits and outsplits.

In this research, we have examined the complex aspect of the Heavy Quark potential, focusing on its dissociation at high temperatures and strong magnetic fields. Our work builds upon previous studies by introducing three distinct features: comprehensive calculations of Landau levels, a novel gauge boson propagator in a magnetized plasma, and an intricate, direction-dependent heavy quark potential. To showcase our advancements, we have generated detailed visualizations, such as heavy quark potential tomography and dissociation probability diagrams, at various temperature and magnetic field conditions.

To effectively answer complex questions, large language models need information about specific entities, but can't store all necessary knowledge themselves, so they rely on external sources like knowledge graphs to fill gaps. Our proposed solution, OREO-LM, includes a special layer that lets a language model work together with a knowledge graph to find the best answer, and in return, the language model becomes more accurate. By integrating OREO-LM with existing language models, such as RoBERTa and T5, we achieved record-breaking results and also got better explanations for the models' choices, thanks to the ability to infer new relationships between entities.

We have developed a novel method of constructing high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of simplicial complexes. Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a vital role in theoretical computer science but unfortunately, there are only a few constructions available that offer arbitrarily small local spectral expansion.

Our research involves presenting a probabilistic algorithm that takes an input high dimensional expander X and generates a sub-complex Y, also a high dimensional expander with infinite covers of bounded-degree simplicial complexes. The generated Y preserves X's graph structure, reducing link complexity and inherits a sparsified form of X's link structure when the link of X has a sparsified form. The basis of this algorithm lies in an efficient isolation procedure that removes edges from X's link, and this method can be extended to isolate independent sets within X's link, independent of X's dimension.

Recent advancements in language models have revealed the potential for outstanding zero-shot performance through cleverly crafted natural language prompts. However, creating effective prompts necessitates considerable trial and error. Consequently, there is a pressing need to determine which qualities of a prompt contribute to successful model performance. To this end, we have collected and standardized a diverse set of prompts designed for specific tasks and tested them on tasks for which they were not initially intended. Our quantitative analysis across multiple tasks indicates that prompts containing answer options and those not used during pre-training demonstrate the highest success rates.

We have computed the Benois $\mathscr{L}$-invariants for weight one cuspforms and their corresponding adjoint representations. Furthermore, our calculations extend Gross' $p$-adic regulator to non-critical Artin motives, which aligns with Deligne's framework. The construction proposed by Benois hinges on the selection of a regular submodule. When the representation is $p$-regular, choosing such a submodule is analogous to selecting a'motivic' $p$-refinement, making the process fairly intuitive. However, when the representation is $p$-irregular, things become more intricate as regular submodules are categorized by a flag variety, resulting in an abundance of choices that involve continuous parameters. Despite these complications, our analysis in select examples highlights how Hida theory and eigencurve geometry can facilitate the identification of a limited set of choices that possess notable arithmetic and'mixed-motivic' significance.

Detecting complex multifrequency microwave (MW) electric fields is difficult 
due to interference from overlapping frequencies. Research using Rydberg 
atoms shows promise in MW radar and communications systems. Yet, the atoms are 
susceptible not only to desired signals, but also to interference from 
atomic interactions and environmental noise. To resolve these challenges, we've 
successfully integrated Rydberg atoms with deep learning algorithms, allowing the 
model to leverage the atoms' sensitivity while minimizing the impact of noise 
without requiring the resolution of complex mathematical equations. In a recent 
experiment, our Rydberg-deep learning system revealed the ability to extract 
information from MW fields with an accuracy five times higher than before, 
using the atoms' sensitivity to detect signals in the range of tens of Hz for 
megahertz frequencies.

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant radial positions. Photoionization models propose that the low-level star formation in UGC 8839 serves as an effective "sticker' that keeps gas in the galaxy, thereby preventing it from escaping. This theoretical framework suggests a connecting role for a dark matter-dominated galaxy to maintain its gravitational hold on its gaseous components.

For a quasiregular self-map in 3D space, research has demonstrated that the Hausdorff dimension of its fast escaping set can be any value within the range of 1 to 3. An estimated lower bound has also been proposed for the Hausdorff dimension of its Julia set under a specific growth constraint.

Using the Neutral Gas Ion Mass Spectrometer on board the Mars Atmospheric and Volatile Evolution/NASA Mars Science Laboratory mission, the oxygen and nitrogen composition of the upper Martian atmosphere is measured. This paper examines the propagation of gravity waves in the upper atmosphere of Mars, using data from various spacecraft including the Mars Global Surveyor, the Mars Odyssey, the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, and the Mars Atmosphere and Volatile Evolution mission. The goal is to understand the impact of these gravity waves on the upper atmosphere using the neutral density measurements available to us. The analysis reveals that the observed neutral density variations are in line with the propagation of gravity waves, with the observed vertical and horizontal scales matching previously reported estimates. Additionally, the model's predicted phase speeds and the observed values show a positive correlation, with the observed values not significantly different from the model's values. The analysis also reveals that the growth rate of the non-linear development of the gravity waves increases with increasing atmospheric density, which could lead to a complete disruption of the upper atmosphere under certain conditions. The data from the three spacecraft is used to investigate the variability of the gravity waves at different scales, with the ODY and MRO data revealing an increase in wave activity in the stratosphere and mesosphere during the winter months, and the MAVEN and MRO data revealing an increase in wave activity in the exosphere and upper atmosphere during the spring and summer months. The LHC holds the record for the highest energy particle collisions, encompassing not only proton-proton and heavy ion interactions but also those of photons with photons and hadrons. This capability stems from the fact that protons and ions within the LHC possess an electromagnetic field, acting as a source of photons, which can then interact either with other photons or with hadrons. Specifically, ultra-peripheral collisions occur when high-energy ions surpass the range of the strong force, enabled by virtual photons exchanged between the nuclei, whose numbers directly correlate with nuclear electric charge. Given its exceptional energy levels, the LHC serves as the most powerful photon source ever constructed, particularly in favouring photoproduction of heavy vector mesons due to their inherent affinity to photons. Recent experiments examining the forward J/psi production in lead-lead ultra-peripheral collisions at 5.02 TeV using the ALICE detector are featured.

Recent breakthroughs in audio generation through visual stimulation involve selecting short, low-quality sounds and using sampling-based methods. However, current models using this approach can't ensure the availability of suitable sounds and often result in poor visual quality. Our work presents a unified model growing a high-quality audio video sequence. Our approach relies on a video-conditioned audio generator producing compact, visually appealing sound snippets that are then expanded into full-length sounds. To improve reliability, we introduce a discriminator evaluating both the logical connection between videos and sounds, and the acoustic quality of produced sounds. Our novel disk-based training strategy avoids the issue of unaligned video and sound lengths during training. By doing so, we achieve significant improvements in the reliability and efficiency of sound generation. Our model grows more than double the length of audio video sequences compared to the state-of-the-art method in the same area, while maintaining comparable visual quality. Our generated content is also preferred by humans over existing approaches, according to a conducted mean opinion score assessment.

Recurrent neural networks have emerged as highly effective algorithms for processing sequential data, including natural languages, sounds, and time-series information. In contrast to conventional feed-forward networks, they incorporate a self-referential mechanism, allowing for the retention of temporal context and the sequential transmission of information. This architecture has enabled exceptional performance in a range of significant tasks such as natural language modeling, stock market forecasting, image description, speech recognition, machine translation, and object tracking. However, the process of training fully connected recurrent networks is complex, involving intricate gradient flow management. To address these challenges, numerous studies have been conducted. This article aims to provide an overview of recurrent neurons, their variations, and expert tips for efficiently training fully recurrent neural networks, drawing from the Multiple Object Tracking module within our Google AI Essentials course.

Achieving a balance between pandemic control and economic considerations is a delicate task, as modeling under specific economic assumptions often yields non-transferable results. This research investigates how implementing timely moderate measures can resolve the trade-off between medical efficacy and economic impact, and attributes this finding to the broader concept of 'economic irreversibility,' illustrating its analogy to the principles of thermodynamics. A fundamental inequality provides a framework for the implementation of such measures. A novel theoretical approach underlying this methodology contributes to the body of econophysics research.

The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue: identifying and resolving data quality problems early on. To address this, a method is developed that calculates the value of individual data records to a machine learning model. This was achieved by creating a data importance evaluation framework based on the Shapley value concept. By representing various data debugging tasks as cooperative games, different algorithms can be utilized to assign importance weights to data records. Based on this, a dataset optimization framework is proposed that helps users prioritize data records for analysis. Additionally, multiple data debugging algorithms are developed that address specific problems such as data labeling, feature selection, and model training. To showcase the efficacy of the proposed framework, experiments were conducted on multiple real-world datasets, and results indicate that it is capable of improving model performance by refining dataset accuracy.

This work reveals underlying relationships between various, seemingly unrelated branches of mathematics: combinatorics, algebraic statistics, topology, and enumerative algebraic geometry. We emphasize discrete invariants, which have strong ties to the foundation of algebraic statistics and provide a mathematical framework for counting betweeen them. Our findings are illustrated by several examples, including the computation of the Euler characteristic, the Okounkov-Volin-Vologodsky $q$-analog, and the number of degree-$d$ maps from $\mathbb{P}^1_\mathbb{C}$ to $\mathbb{P}^1_\mathbb{C}$.

This study provides an in-depth examination of how high pressure influences the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn, an antiferromagnetic compound with a triangular structure. Theoretical models predict that when exposed to pressure, Mn$_3$Sn undergoes a significant transformation, where the distances between certain atoms in the material change significantly, stabilizing a helical magnetic ground state. Experiments have demonstrated that at pressures exceeding 1.5 GPa, the material's anomalous Hall effect is entirely eliminated. The pressure-dependent magnetization study revealed that as pressure increased, Mn$_3$Sn shifted from a conventional antiferromagnetic ground state to a helical state, where a required characteristic for the anomalous Hall effect is absent. X-ray diffraction experiments indicate that this phenomenon is not caused by structural changes within the material. The investigation further reveals that when Mn$_3$Sn enters the helical state, its in-plane lattice parameter exhibits unusual temperature dependence, supporting the hypothesis that atom rearrangement significantly affects the material's properties. Ultimately, this research significantly contributes to understanding the interplay between pressure and magnetic ground states in Mn$_3$Sn and its related compounds.

Formal knowledge acquisition is pivotal for developing artificial intelligence (AI)
capable of human-level cognition, with semantic relationships between entities being
one essential aspect of it. In the realm of Natural Language Processing (NLP), Relation
Extraction (RE), a subset of information extraction, plays a crucial role in acquiring
this vital knowledge automatically from natural language texts. By automatically
identifying semantic relationships between entities, RE contributes significantly to the
domain. Notably, recent studies have established Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) as the
prevalent approach for RE. In particular, the reliability of DNNs in the forms of
supervised and distant supervision methods makes them highly sought-after solutions
for RE. This article serves as an introduction, offering an in-depth analysis of DNNs in
RE from two primary angles: supervised RE and distant supervision RE. It also covers
the emergence of new approaches, recent trends, and prospective avenues for further
research in the area of RE.

This paper delves into a Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian in a particular class of annular domains. Specifically, we examine a setup involving a larger open set $\Omega_0$, a smaller ball of radius $r$, and consider a first eigenvalue in this scenario where both the Steklov and Robin boundary conditions are imposed. We then analyze the main features of the eigenvalue and its associated eigenfunctions, as well as how the parameter $\beta$ and $r$ influence the behavior of the eigenvalue when they vary.

We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks are more effectively modeled as hypergraphs, yet their associated datasets are often presented as projected graphs. To better comprehend this phenomenon, we establish a theoretical framework to examine its underlying principles and worst-case scenarios. This framework informs our proposal of supervised hypergraph reconstruction, a novel task aimed at recovering a real-world hypergraph from its graph projection using domain-specific knowledge. To achieve this, we develop a method that involves two components: first, a sampling strategy is employed to significantly reduce the large number of potential hyperedges; second, a hyperedge classifier with two optimized variants is designed to identify candidate hyperedges based on their structural properties in the graph projection. Our experiments validate the efficacy of our approach and its extensions, with impressive results that outperform baseline methods by a significant margin in accuracy, particularly on difficult datasets. Our implementation and data are freely available for download.

In medical radiology reports, doctors document vital information about patients'
health conditions. Their findings are derived from analyzing raw imaging data and
describe the inner workings of the human body. Preparing these reports necessitates
medical imaging experts to be familiar with both normal anatomical structures and
diseases, enabling them to identify abnormalities and describe them accurately.
Understanding medical report interpretation is essential for several applications,
such as automatic image analysis and content extraction. Current medical report
interpretation methods, however, struggle with detailing findings due to the
limited context available, resulting in inadequate understanding of the human body's
anatomical structures. To tackle this issue, researchers propose utilizing raw
medical images to supplement text-based report information, allowing for a
more comprehensive interpretation of the human body's structures. To test this
approach, they developed a multi-part dataset consisting of radiology reports,
their corresponding detailed annotations, and image analysis results. The dataset
includes both unstructured and semi-structured report types and covers a range of
anatomical areas. To establish a baseline for comparison, they also designed
evaluation criteria and conducted initial experiments to evaluate how the proposed
two-part representation affects report interpretation. The dataset and its
implementation techniques are made publicly accessible to facilitate further
research and experimentation.

Bill Thurston initially found that Euler classes of taut foliations in hyperbolic 3-manifolds have a limited range and then made an educated guess that this range is the absolute minimum. Subsequent work by a different researcher, collaborating with David Gabai, found counterexamples that contradict this theory. Due to the connection between tight contact structures and taut foliations, researchers now consider the possibility that this theory could hold for tight contact structures, which are also related to Euler classes of one. To test this idea, recent findings show that previously found counterexamples are also related to tight contact structures, leaving room for the possibility that this theory might be correct for tight contact structures.

We propose an advanced concept for measuring directional emission in microcavity lasers. Initially, entropy in the polar far-field profile effectively gauges the degree of unidirectional light release, outperforming previous methods which struggle with variation. Secondly, we introduce a phenomenological angle for measuring emission directionality, but its practical application is limited to straightforward cases due to the inability to handle complex structures. Conversely, entropy based on semi-marginal probability in the Cartesian coordinate achieves comparable results and is also adaptable to emissions with complex structures.

Our findings provide concrete evidence for the stability of cryptocurrencies as a medium of exchange. Between 2016 and 2020, the prices of major cryptocurrencies remained steady when compared to other significant financial assets. After isolating shorter price fluctuations lasting less than a month, we analyzed the daily returns in US dollars of leading cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Ripple, alongside their respective counterparts, Gold, Silver, and the Total Cryptocurrencies index. To evaluate the stability of filtered daily returns, we applied three distinct measures. Firstly, the Pearson correlation coefficients between the analyzed assets showed a notable increase in 2020, reaching levels similar to those observed in traditional financial markets. Secondly, the results of our dynamic time-warping analysis, which permits both leads and lags in relation to our benchmark, revealed the existence of systematic patterns in cryptocurrency price movements. Lastly, the significant decline in our time series data's variability, as evidenced by the standard deviation of total cryptocurrencies returns in late 2020, demonstrates a considerable reduction in volatility. Our research lays the groundwork for a new area of study, which we term 'Cryptology,' and suggests numerous applications for the proposed concept.

By integrating analytical methods including field theory, probability and integrability, we resolve the large deviation issue of the KPZ equation at early time periods. Expanding the existing weak noise theory, which reformulates large deviations into a related nonlinear problem, we reveal that the resulting nonlinear equation shares similarities with experts have noted with the Zakharov-Shabat system's inverse scattering problem. Utilizing the inherent structures within integrable systems, we establish the exact coefficients needed to replicate either the KPZ or inverse scattering equations. Since the nonlinear equation can be solved through conventional integrability tools, this yields the rare event probability estimates required to answer the initial question. Our approach extends the bounds of applicability for both the weak noise theory and the method of inflated probabilities, enabling the estimation of rare events even when the noise level exceeds the typical range. Lastly, by interpreting the nonlinear equation as a hydrodynamic type, we reveal the underlying causes for the observed extreme events, which stem from a complex interaction between the leading wave and its weaker counterparts.

The solar wind's compressive plasma turbulence at sub-ion scales is analyzed with data from the Magnetospheric MultiScale mission. Utilizing both the Fast Plasma Investigation instrument and calibrated spacecraft potential measurements from the Spin Plane Double Probe, researchers are able to investigate turbulent patterns down to specific frequencies. These measurements are then applied to various solar wind plasma intervals. One such interval is scrutinized, yielding valuable insights into its power spectral density fluctuations spanning from the inertial to sub-ion range. Two possible explanations for these density patterns exist, suggesting that they are a result either of specific wave types and interactions at varying scales or a broader physical phenomenon, the Hall effect. These theories are substantiated through the examination of associated electric field data.

In SASE FEL schemes, short pulse durations are commonly limited by the coherence time, typically measuring in hundreds of attoseconds for hard X-rays and femtoseconds for softer ranges. This paper introduces a modification to the chirp-taper technique allowing for overcoming coherence time restrictions. Simulation data for the FLASH facility show successful production of pulses lasting several hundred attoseconds within a 2-10 nm wavelength, yielding high peak powers of hundreds of megawatts, with a potential for delivering over a thousand pulses per second to enable groundbreaking attosecond science applications.

A mathematical model examining the impact of turbulence on a stratified flow is investigated, incorporating eddy coefficients that influence viscosity but neglect those affecting diffusivity. By combining both vertical and horizontal viscosity factors, a fourth-order Taylor-Goldstein differential equation arises to describe vertical velocity perturbations, reducing to a modified equation when only the latter factor is considered under inviscid conditions. Assuming that key parameters are slowly changing, geometrical and physical approximations are explored for this modified equation using the WKB method near critical levels and singularities, including turning points.

Election manipulation through the alteration of voting district boundaries constitutes
a long-standing issue in democracy, yet detecting it has been challenging due to
the absence of clear analytical evidence. To address this concern, we developed a
method combining Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Simulated Annealing to quantify the
level of unfairness in a districting plan. Our results show the effectiveness of
this approach in identifying biased voting district boundaries in the United States.
Specifically, our research focuses on Texas, where it highlights districts with high
levels of partisan bias. Using the calculated unfairness metrics, we ranked all Texas
districting plans since 2011 and found many had significant imbalance, with some exceeding
the state's legal limits by large margins.

A novel defect detection approach for patterned fabric images utilizes a direction-sensitive feature descriptor, GHOG, which integrates Gabor and HOG to precisely locate defects. Since defects distort the fabric's uniform pattern orientation, this method leverages the direction awareness to effectively identify the defect region. Following the development of a directional descriptor, the proposed technique applies low-rank decomposition to differentiate the background from defect information within the fabric's image blocks. A nonconvex surrogate function and an alternative direction method of multipliers (ADMM) are utilized to improve the low-rank decomposition model's efficiency and computation speed. Ultimately, the sparse matrix-derived saliency map is segmented to pinpoint defect regions. Experimental findings demonstrate that this method outperforms existing techniques and successfully detects fabric defects.

To enhance the robustness of target-driven visual navigation systems powered by deep reinforcement learning, we introduce an information-theoretic constraint to the learning process. By maximizing the correlation between the agent's navigation actions and the resulting visual transformations, the agent makes more informed decisions, effectively learning a predictive model of the environment. Through a variational generative approach, the agent learns to simulate the impact of its actions, leveraging this understanding to forecast the outcome of different navigational choices and select the most suitable path. Experimental results demonstrate that this guided navigation system yields exceptional performance in virtual challenges and even generalizes remarkably well to unfamiliar environments and target types, outperforming current state-of-the-art models substantially.

For asymptotically flat spacetimes, where light is emitted at a distance from the gravitational source, research indicates that the Bondi mass aspect must satisfy specific requirements to reach the point of infinity without obstruction. In general relativity, such constraints result in an upper limit on the mass change rate in relation to the speed of light and gravitational constant, leading to an interesting insight into Dyson's maximum luminosity theorem. In contrast, the conditions under which scalar gravitational waves in Brans-Dicke theory allow light to escape infinity without being overpowered by rapid mass loss.

We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centres of galaxies and 5-50% of these will merge in nuclear star clusters at high redshifts. These events peak at z=5-7 with a merger rate of 0.4-10 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our predictions also reveal that the most massive of these remnants primarily reside in small, low-mass nuclear star clusters formed in the early universe. These clusters host black holes of masses 40-85 M_\\odot that can produce detections similar to GW190521, specifically in a mass range typically found for pulsational pair-instability supernovae with a merger rate of 0.01-0.09 years^-1 Gpc^-3.

In modern power distribution networks equipped with energy storage systems (ESS) and advanced control systems, the standard monitoring and protection systems are not optimized for identifying malfunctions in smart devices. This work presents a novel data-driven method for identifying critical incidents related to ESS performance in distribution networks. Our approach relies on the connections between sensor data streams and does not necessitate prior knowledge of the system or parameters. It also features a data enrichment component that enables the detection of incidents even when data is limited. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through detailed case studies that focus on active and reactive power control strategies for ESS.

Our study focuses on how the $\rho$ and $\omega$ mesons contribute to the radiative decays $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ and $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi\gamma$. The first process is predominantly driven by the $\omega$ meson. On the other hand, the cascade decays involving the $\rho$ and $\omega$ mesons are substantially suppressed compared to other diagrams, specifically those that go through the $\psi(2S)$ or a three-body decay of $\rho$. The measured branching ratios for $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ and $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi\gamma$ are potentially within reach for the BESIII and LHCb Collaborations. The $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ and $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi\pi^+\pi^- \gamma$ decays may be used to determine the couplings $g_{X\psi\omega}$ and $g_{X\psi\rho}$, respectively, which would offer insight into the isoscalar and isovector components of the X(3872) wave function.

We provide a characterization of smooth quadrics based on the existence of full exceptional collections with a specific property, generalizing a previous result obtained by C. Vial for projective spaces.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months.

The study on varying electron spin orientation employs the coordinate transformation method. Characteristically, Topological Insulators exhibit an uneven spin orientation shift within the Brillouin zone. In cases of defects, this shift occurs along closed paths in real space, with both instances characterized by non-trivial spin connections. This approach is utilized to determine the spin connections of three-dimensional Topological Insulators containing topological defects. The edge dislocation on the surface of a Topological Insulator generates a spin connection controlled by torsion, allowing electrons to move in confined circular areas and two-dimensional regions. The edge dislocations break parity symmetry, producing a current measured by the in-plane spin component on the surface, with this current accompanied by a tunneling density of states calculation for edge dislocations.

Consider the scenario where $p$ lies between 1 and infinity, $
u$ ranges between 0.5 and infinity, and $\mathcal{S}_
u$ denotes the set of non-zero vectors in 2D space with a polar angle smaller than $ rac{\pi}{2
u}$. We introduce $R > 0$, and $\omega_p(x)$ as the p-harmonic measure of $\partial B(0,R) \cap \mathcal{S}_
u$ at point $x$, relative to the ball $B(0,R)\cap \mathcal{S}_
u$. We show that for some constant $C$, $\omega_p(x)$ satisfies a specific inequality with respect to the exponent $k(
u,p)$, where the exponent depends on both $
u$ and $p$, and use this estimate to derive local growth rates for p-subharmonic and p-superharmonic functions within certain domains which resemble sectors. These estimates also provide bounds on the rate of convergence near domain boundaries featuring an inward or outward pointed cusp, and consequently imply the existence of a scale-invariant limit function, denoted as $\omega_{
u,p}$, which represents the p-harmonic measure of a unit vector $e$, relative to the set $\{0\} < e$ in the real projective plane.

Using a joint multivariate spatial model based on the work of Heffernan and Tawn, the relationship between satellite wind speed data, wave height observations, and extreme weather patterns is examined in the North East Atlantic between 2007-2018. A template-based approach is used to compare and combine wind and wave data from satellites and historical forecasts. Analysis involves standardizing wind and wave measurements and applying an extreme value model to estimate the probability of severe storms in specific locations. Results from this investigation reveal a significant decline in extreme weather correlations among Metop satellite wind speeds, wave forecasts, and wave measurements over a range of 600 to 800 kilometers.

Inspired by intermediate Lang conjectures concerning hyperbolicity and rational points, we establish new theorems on the finiteness of non-constant morphism sets from a specific fixed variety to another, also defined over a specific number field, by adapting Faltings's work on the finiteness of maps in moduli spaces.

A key concept called manipulability ellipsoids effectively encodes human pose data and task-dependent information, significantly contributing to teaching robots human-like motion through emulation. In robotics literature, there has been a recent shift towards transfer learning between robots. However, the transfer of this information from human to robot systems has been overlooked. This research aims to bridge this knowledge gap with a new method to transfer manipulability information from one robot to another with a different kinematic structure. Since these ellipsoids are based on symmetric positive-definite matrices, they can be treated as points on a specific geometric manifold. This work offers the first approach to transfer manipulability by leveraging the technique of point cloud registration. To achieve this, it employs an algorithm combining parallel transport with Iterative Closest Point. The method also relies on constructing a manipulability cone surface, representing task-dependent information, which can be adapted using ICN-based point cloud matching. The method's effectiveness has been validated through experiments involving adaptation from human to robotic arms.

To study non-resonant Higgs boson pair production in the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel at the LHC using the matrix element method, we examine how to differentiate the Higgs boson pair signal from the dominant irreducible top quark pair background. Specifically, our analysis focuses on final states with two leptons and assesses the effectiveness of separating signal and background for experimental conditions representative of the ATLAS and CMS experiments during LHC Run 2, leveraging the DELPHES simulation package. As a result, we were able to achieve a $0.26\%$ top quark pair background suppression, corresponding to a $35\%$ Higgs boson pair signal efficiency.

A novel method is introduced for training single-view 3D object pose estimation models, utilizing unstructured, 'in-the-wild' video footage where objects are rotated. These scenes are common and can be readily captured using smartphones. Traditional training datasets are costly to create and consist of controlled, standardized sequences. In contrast, our approach leverages the inherent variability in unstructured videos, effectively translating real-world accidental recordings into robust pose estimation models. By incorporating a data augmentation technique that mimics the unstructured video distribution, pre-trained models can be developed. We utilize these models to automatically collect a large, diverse dataset of unstructured videos, which in turn further enhances the models' performance, while also outperforming existing methods on standard benchmarks in direct training scenarios. Moreover, our approach facilitates the simultaneous estimation of object class and pose, achieving class-agnostic results that set a new benchmark for single-view estimations.

Despite widespread vaccination, a substantial number of people still harbor doubts due to misconceptions disseminated through social media regarding COVID-19 vaccines. Misinformation spread online does not necessarily lead to the adoption of false information; in fact, a proposed novel framework can discern one's attitude toward this misinformation. This new framework leverages neural networks and attitude consistency to classify stances on COVID-19 vaccine-related misinformation. A novel neural framework, utilizing knowledge graphs to organize stances, successfully identifies attitudes toward this misinformation with outstanding results, outperforming other current approaches. Experiments were conducted on the recently created CoVaxLies dataset, a comprehensive collection of COVID-19 vaccine-related misinformation gathered from Twitter discussions. This new dataset allows us to distinguish which specific types of misinformation are more commonly accepted and which are more commonly disputed.

Advancements in attosecond science hold great potential to unveil the core electronic behavior of matter, contingent on achieving two interconnected technological milestones linked to high-order harmonic generation sources. Firstly, achieving a higher photon flux would allow researchers to measure even the faintest electronic processes, while also attaining better spectral tunability would grant selectivity in targeting specific electronic transitions. Breakthroughs are made feasible by parametric waveform synthesis, giving scientists the capability to craft controllable, highly-tunable high-energy electric transients. Our findings demonstrate that by manipulating the waveform of the driving laser pulse via its relative phase and carrier-envelope phase, it's possible to exert fine-grained control over attosecond pulse characteristics. This innovation not only amplifies experimental possibilities in the realm of attosecond science, but also paves the way for a highly sophisticated, coherent manipulation of free-electron paths.

Eclipse predictions for binary stars can be significantly improved by revising older data that is no longer accurate. This involves accounting for potential companions that can create recurring periods in time shifts. A study discovered a low probability (0.00005%) of detecting new companions using eclipse time shifts. Researchers analyzed data on Algol ($\beta$ Persei) and found tentative signs of up to five additional companion candidates, which are believed to have orbital periods ranging from 1.863 to 219 years. These signals are consistent across 236 years of data and also matched the first 226.2 years of the data, accurately predicting eclipses for the following 9.2 years. The companion candidates' orbital planes are thought to be aligned due to the stable and unchanging eclipses of Algol since the early observations of Goodricke (1783).

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the same optimal blow-up criterion found by Holmer and Roudenko for solutions in an infinite domain. A previously established approach, derived by Glassey through the concavity of variance, is not applicable in this context due to the appearance of boundary terms of undesirable sign in the second derivative of variance. Our primary argument introduces a new, modified variance measure, bounded from below and concave in a way that is relevant for solutions in this particular scenario.

Physics-informed neural networks offer an innovative solution for partial differential equations that combines adaptability and efficient incorporation of observed data. Despite achieving significant success across a wide array of differential equations, further improvements to computational efficiency are required for this approach. To address this need, enhancing training point generation is an important direction of investigation. Both adaptive and quasi-uniform sampling techniques have previously been explored, each showing benefits. To leverage these insights, we introduce Residual-based Adaptive Node Generation, which combines an adjustable nodal distribution method and a memory mechanism. We then conduct experiments on both linear and nonlinear PDEs, evaluating its accuracy and efficiency relative to traditional sampling methods.

This study examines the behavior and simulation of multi-domain ferroelectric FETs by analyzing the oscillations in their electrostatic conduction band profile, which are characteristic of these devices. We model these dynamics by solving coupled two-dimensional Poisson's equations and energy equations, and find that the system converges to a stable thermodynamic state through energy minimization. Our analysis also shows that the movement of domain walls within the ferroelectric material leads to the negative capacitance effect, which in turn affects the device's drain current and variability due to the domain period. We also investigated how the domain wall's soft or hard state transition influences the device's electrical properties and transport. Our simulations are verified through both experimental data and phase-field modeling.

A significant knowledge gap exists in understanding the Cargo ecosystem's architecture and how vulnerability dissemination occurs within it. Existing studies that generalize security management approaches across multiple ecosystems often overlook the unique technical characteristics of individual ecosystems, hindering direct applicability of security governance strategies to Cargo. To address this disparity, this research employs knowledge graph techniques to construct a dependency vulnerability graph for Cargo and presents an innovative algorithm to identify vulnerability dissemination paths and scope. By conducting a comprehensive empirical study on Cargo's ecosystem, this research investigates vulnerability traits, propagation extent, and factors influencing vulnerability dissemination, revealing that Cargo's security vulnerabilities primarily stem from memory-related issues. Notably, 18% of libraries still harbor vulnerabilities even after updating to the latest version, while 19.78% of Cargo's ecosystem versions tend to be vulnerable. This study's findings offer actionable insights for Cargo administrators, developers, and library owners to effectively manage library updates, ultimately enhancing the ecosystem's overall security and reliability.

For analyzing ergodic properties in stochastic dynamical systems, it's essential to demonstrate irreducibility. This paper confirms the irreducibility of stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations subjected to discrete jump noises and shows these results apply universally, imposing minimal restrictions on noise conditions. A critical factor in this study is the authors' and T. Zhang's previously established criteria for irreducibility in stochastic equations with jump noises. This proof is then utilized to demonstrate ergodic behavior in stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations and includes scenarios of weak dissipation with jump degenerate noise.

For a finite noncyclic nilpotent group G, we're analyzing the minimal vertex degree in its power graph. This power graph connects vertices based on one being a positive power of the other. By examining the group's prime divisors and Sylow subgroups, we've pinpointed vertices related to its cyclic subgroups. This allows us to establish a connection between the group's properties and its minimal vertex degree in the power graph. This study provides degree calculations for specific types of noncyclic abelian groups.

Hadron-hadron collisions in the intermediate Feynman-x region (between 0.1 and 0.9) have not been extensively studied at high-energy ranges above sqrt(s) = 63 GeV using the CERN Intersecting Storage Rings. I explore a feasible method to investigate this at the Large Hadron Collider operating at sqrt(s) = 13 TeV, an equivalent increase in fixed-target energy of 40,000 times, with crucial implications for understanding the characteristics of cosmic ray showers.

Deep learning models, specifically Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), are capable of generating robust image representations, but are limited when dealing with orientation transformations. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel model, Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs), based on Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs), which can learn representations that are less sensitive to orientation changes. By combining LGFs with standard DCNNs, our OCNs can leverage the benefits of existing deep learning frameworks while improving their robustness to orientation changes. Our proposed LGFs are constructed by selecting key Gabor filters and expressing them as sparse linear combinations of these markers, utilizing a matrix factorization framework with sparsity and low-rank constraints to integrate local and global structures. Through the propagation of this low-rank structure, our method achieves significantly improved sparsity for representing the original Gabor filter bank. Our experimental results show that OCNs outperform existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and computational cost, with a significant reduction in model complexity.

This study seeks to enhance the computational efficiency of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) in point cloud learning. We critically examine the conventional graph convolution, comprising a KNN search and a multilayer perceptron. By dissecting its underlying mathematical operations, we arrive at two key insights for GCN optimization. Firstly, the 3D point cloud representation's geometric structure is efficiently propagated across the GCN through KNN search. This insight drives the simplification of multiple KNN searches within GCNs. Secondly, rearranging the sequence of feature aggregation and multilayer perceptron operations yields equivalent results. Based on these findings, we refine the computational procedure for GCNs. Experimental results demonstrate the optimized networks enjoy lower memory requirements, accelerated iteration speeds, and improved generalization capabilities in ablation studies and point cloud classification benchmarks. The simplified networks exhibit reduced memory usage, faster inference speed, and equivalent or improved accuracy compared to baseline methods.

We introduce a groundbreaking type of Trojan attack, which uses fixed images in conceptual meaning but can take various forms visually. Unlike existing Trojan attacks, which embed inconsequential triggers in clean images, our method considers trigger images as the fundamental representation of its trigger class. As our backdoor trigger is triggered by any image related to the target class, it's inherently connected to that concept. This makes our method more applicable and easier to implement, as it doesn't rely on manually selecting trigger images. Instead, it uses network features to find them. We've tested our method on multiple datasets and show its superiority over existing Trojan attacks.

We are developing an image slicer for an integral field unit, ROSIE IFU, to integrate with the IMACS spectrograph on the Magellan Baade Telescope at the Las Campanas Observatory. By splitting the 50.4 x 53.5 field of view into four subfields, and further segmenting these into 21 individual 0.6 x 53.5 slices, we'll achieve four pseudo-slits, spaced six arcminutes apart. This will allow for a spectral range of 1800 Angstroms with a resolution of 2000. Our current progress includes preparing the optics, coating the first slicer, crafting the mounts, and writing the software, all aiming to enhance IMACS's functionality by facilitating the efficient observation of extended objects like galaxies.

In this paper, the carbon-carbon fusion research is revisited to incorporate the latest developments. Specifically, key experimental and theoretical findings from a recent analysis by Beck {\it et al.} (Eur. Phys. J. A {\bf 56}, 97 (2020)) are considered to outline the pathway for enhancing low-energy astrophysical $S$-factor determinations via new Threshold Hand Mirror (THHM) measurements.

A crucial aspect of discovering and studying exoplanets is identifying terrestrial planets resembling Earth. New studies emphasize the significance of considering volatile depletion in star composition to predict the bulk composition and internal structures of these planets. In this research, we apply this concept to a sample of 13 stars that host terrestrial planets similar to our Sun, utilising high-precision data on their elemental composition. Based on this and other constraints, we simulated the detailed mineral makeup and internal structures of hypothetical habitable-zone exoplanets around these stars. Our model indicates that most of these planets are expected to have compositions and internal structures analogous to those of Earth. However, our analysis reveals two exceptions, the Kepler-10 and Kepler-37 planets, which would likely develop cores significantly smaller than Earth due to oxidation. Furthermore, our exploration of this devolatilisation model's boundaries and variation in planetary mass and size highlights the potential diversity of internal structures in terrestrial planets. By combining precise star abundances, devolatilisation, and planetary mass and size considerations, our study advances understanding of terrestrial exoplanet interior structures, which are pivotal in grasping planetary evolution and dynamics.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become a preferred method for wireless localization based on channel state information (CSI), utilizing raw CSI to learn location-specific features. Nevertheless, several studies demonstrate that CSI is prone to system disturbances and subtle environmental changes. Designing handcrafted features can also restrict the potential of channel representation learning by the DNN. This research suggests attention-based CSI for learning robust features. The proposed approach's efficacy in centralized and distributed massive MIMO systems is assessed using ray-tracing channels in two railway environments under varying conditions, resulting in a superior performance compared to a conventional DNN.

This paper presents a comprehensive framework for modal logic semantics by linking different types of logical meaning in the literature to the topological categories theory. Building on similar methods in categorical logic, we will thoroughly examine the relationship between the structural composition of the modal language, its various expansions, and the topological structures in categories, thus offering an abstract understanding of the underlying logical framework.

A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, effectively mirroring the requirements of a certain vertex coloring in a transformed version of the graph. This notion was initially proposed as an open problem by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1990, assuming a bipartite graph of high enough girth and a specific degree constraint could be colored using a certain number of colors, but in 2021 this was contested. Now, another example is given which also contests the conjecture originally presented by those authors.

We investigate functions defined on the vertices of the Hamming graphs H(n,q), focusing specifically on those with support contained in the direct sum of the eigenspaces U_i(n,q), U_{i+1}(n,q),..., U_j(n,q) where 0 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ n. Under certain conditions, specifically when n is greater than or equal to the sum of i and j, and when the size of the alphabet is 3 or greater, we identify the functions with minimum possible support and establish a characterization for those with such a minimum. In scenarios where n is less than the sum of i and j, but with a sufficiently large alphabet size of at least 4, we identify similar properties of functions. In particular, we establish a characterization for the functions within the eigenspace U_i(n,q) with minimum possible support in several specific scenarios.

COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but users had to run it locally as a standalone application. To address this limitation, we developed ShinyCOPASI, a web-based platform allowing users to interact with COPASI models through their web browser. Built with R using CoRC and Shiny, ShinyCOPASI mirrors COPASI's interface for seamless exploration and enables running tasks available in the original software within a browser. It offers a basic model upload feature and a server-loaded model option, providing web access to existing models. Users can access ShinyCOPASI at http://shiny.copasi.org/ and the source code at https://github.com/copasi/shinyCOPASI.

Deep neural networks are fundamentally altering the landscape of how data and physical laws are combined, resolving complex problems in physics and engineering that had proven insurmountable with conventional methods. Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves more complicated than traditional methods. This difficulty arises from not only the random fluctuations inherent to noisy data but also limitations imposed by data quantity, model specifications, hyperparameters, optimization techniques, sampling, and overfitting. Despite some recent efforts to quantify uncertainty within NNs, no overarching framework effectively addresses uncertainty quantification even in relatively simple cases such as function approximation. Moreover, most existing research focuses on specific techniques rather than a broad range of methods to quantify uncertainty. In our study, we devise an extensive framework for evaluating different techniques and select seven methods to test across multiple scenarios. Our work serves as a foundation for future uncertainty quantification research, providing a comprehensive evaluation of various approaches and highlighting the significance of method comparison.

We are investigating quantum group analogues of the free group factors' radial subalgebras, specifically those of class functions, within the context of compact quantum groups. We found that the algebras of class functions for the free orthogonal quantum groups cannot be maximally abundant *-subalgebras (MASAs) under certain conditions. Central to our research is the concept of a quasi-split inclusion. We demonstrated that the inclusion of the class functions' algebra is quasi-split in certain unitary quantum group scenarios. Additionally, we showed that the resulting subalgebra is non-abelian. We obtained another key finding related to its relative commutant in such instances. This paper also presents related conclusions for the free discrete-tilde quantum groups.

Policy iteration comes with computational drawbacks in large-scale Markov decision processes due to a local quadratic contraction rate and the costliness of its iterations for many states. Informed by its relation to the semismooth Newton method and the efficiency of its inexact variations, inexact policy iteration, a class of algorithms for large-scale finite MDPs with local contraction guarantees, was introduced. This method is further exemplified through inexact GMRES policy iteration, which applies GMRES for the policy evaluation process. Notably, inexact GMRES policy iteration outperforms policy iteration and optimistic policy iteration by 5.8 and 2.2 times, respectively, in a 10000-state MDP.

Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. We establish in this study that the symbolic and ordinary power series of $I(\mathcal{D})$ share the same equivalence for a specific subclass of weighted directed trees. Moreover, the paper also identifies both the required and sufficient conditions under which the symbolic and ordinary power series of oriented line segments exhibit equal behavior.

This paper examines the solution to an inverse problem presented by expensive computer simulations of complex real-life scenarios. Specifically, researchers focused on an expensive hydrological model designed to generate realistic data for Athens, Georgia, USA. To efficiently handle the large datasets produced by such simulators, an approach involves first selecting key points to approximate the output, and then applying a specialized method to estimate optimal input parameters at those points, while accounting for any uncertainty in the solution. A comprehensive simulation-based study compares the proposed technique with other established methods on a range of synthetic and real-world scenarios.

Research has shown that certain distributional assumptions are required to guarantee the reliable learnability of complex concepts when evaluating a robust model's accuracy and considering the influence of random example exposure, according to Gourdeau et al. (2019). Our paper focuses on the development of new algorithms for learning robust models, where the learner has more flexibility due to the use of local queries. We create the first distribution-free algorithms for achieving robust empirical risk minimization (ERM), a robust measure of model accuracy. Our first learning model utilizes local membership queries under the uniform hazard rate distribution and offers a better factor dependence than previously established methods. Additionally, we developed an innovative learning model that leverages non-uniform local membership queries under the weak distributional assumption, resulting in a better factor dependence than the existing best known approach. To further broaden the applicability of local queries, we designed two new robust learning model algorithms based on local constraint queries without distributional assumptions, resulting in a factor dependence that outperforms existing approaches for binary concepts. Our work addresses a crucial question left unanswered by Gourdeau et al. (2019): Are local queries sufficient for the reliable learning of arbitrary pattern languages. The answer is affirmative, as we have successfully designed a robust learning model based on local membership queries under the uniform hazard rate distribution, offering a better factor dependence than established methods.

For the first time, fragmentation functions for jets associated with a lone photon have been measured in collisions involving protons and a lead-lead nucleus. This analysis used data from the CMS detector at the CERN LHC, operating at a proton-proton center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV. The fragmentation functions for jets above 30 GeV were determined in events with a high-transverse-momentum photon, above 60 GeV, where charged particles with a minimum transverse momentum of 1 GeV were tracked within a narrow cone around the jet axis. By pairing with a high-transverse-momentum photon, the trajectory of the parent parton can be well constrained. In central lead-lead collisions, variations in fragmentation functions compared to those measured in proton-proton collisions were detected, however, little deviation was seen in collisions occurring outside the 50% most central range. Jets within the central lead-lead events exhibited a higher yield of low-energy particles, paired with a decrease in high-transverse-momentum particles, roughly transitioning at a point around 3 GeV. This study is the first to demonstrate alterations in parton (dominated by quarks) showers traversing the QGP with a known initial trajectory, also offering a controlled comparison to test theoretical models.

Recent research involving Feynman integrals has highlighted the significance of Apéry-type inverse binomial series. Building upon previous findings that non-alternating central binomial series could be solved using level four multiple zeta values, we now show that alternating versions require level eight and can be solved using an alternative approach. This involves the substitution of hyperbolic trigonometric 1-forms for their standard trigonometric counterparts.

Follow-up research on WISEA J153429.75-104303.3, previously reported by Meisner et al in 2020, has yielded an assortment of peculiar attributes.
